templates.title: Upload success per app version and network type, resumed attempts counted once
templates.subtopic: collapsing attempts to one row per entity, first-row attributes, inclusive time bounds, exclusion by state

sections.scenario: Creators upload videos from phones on Wi-Fi, 5G and 4G, and an upload interrupted by a dropped connection resumes later, sometimes on a different network. A mobile team wants to know whether a new app version made uploads more reliable, and the agreed measure for this exercise is simple: the share of uploads published within one hour of the first attempt. Every attempt writes one row to the attempt log, and resumed attempts share the upload's upload_id. Counting rows instead of uploads would reward a version that interrupts more often.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns app_version, network_type, uploads, published_within_1h, success_rate, one row per app version and network type that has at least one counted upload, ordered by app_version, network_type. An upload is all the attempts with one upload_id, counted once, under the app_version and network_type of its first attempt (the earliest started_at). An upload is published if one of its attempts has outcome = 'published'; that attempt's ended_at is the publish time. It counts in published_within_1h if the publish time is at most one hour after the first attempt's started_at (exactly one hour counts). success_rate is published_within_1h / uploads, rounded to 4 decimal places. {{draft_rule}} {{id_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). The sample has {{uploads}} uploads in {{attempts}} attempt rows. An upload has at most one published attempt, and no two attempts of one upload start at the same instant.
sections.assumptions: Versions, networks, attempts and the one-hour rule are hypothetical and defined for this exercise only; they do not describe any product's reporting. The log carries no creator or video content, only opaque ids, and the result is aggregated.
sections.criteria: One row per upload before counting; the version and network of the first attempt by started_at; the hour measured from the first attempt, inclusive at exactly one hour; abandoned drafts excluded while drafts published later stay (Hard+); first attempt by time, not by id (Very Hard); correct rounding and order; can discuss confounding by market and in-progress uploads.

clarifications.q: An upload started on 4G and finished on Wi-Fi after a resume. Which network is it?
clarifications.a: 4G: the network of its first attempt.

clarifications.q: Is the hour measured from the attempt that published?
clarifications.a: No. From the started_at of the upload's first attempt, however many resumes came between.

clarifications.q: Published exactly 60 minutes after the first attempt started?
clarifications.a: It counts. One second later does not.

clarifications.q: Do uploads that failed and never published count?
clarifications.a: Yes, in uploads and not in published_within_1h.

clarifications.q: How is the rate rounded?
clarifications.a: ROUND(…, 4) on a numeric.

hints: Reduce the attempts to one row per upload_id first; everything after that counts uploads, not attempts.
(ARRAY_AGG(app_version ORDER BY started_at))[1] or DISTINCT ON (upload_id) … ORDER BY upload_id, started_at gives the first attempt's attributes.
Hard: decide per upload whether it was ever saved as a draft and whether it was ever published, then filter.
Very Hard: order by started_at, never by attempt_id.
followups: The team wants the median minutes from first attempt to publish per version, for published uploads only. Add it and say why it must be read next to the success rate.
Version 2 shipped to Wi-Fi-heavy markets first. How could that make it look more reliable than it is, and how would you compare versions fairly?
Uploads still in progress when the report runs have no final outcome yet. How do you keep the latest hours from looking like failures?
At hundreds of millions of attempts a day, attempts of one upload arrive over hours and days. How would you maintain the per-upload row incrementally, and when is an upload's outcome final?

rules.ask: An upload was interrupted twice and then published. How many rows does your count give it, and how many uploads is it?
MIN or MAX of a text column gives the alphabetically first value, not the first attempt's. Which attempt does your query take the network from?
Is attempt_id guaranteed to follow time? What happens when a phone that was offline sends its first attempt's log late?
An upload publishes exactly one hour after its first attempt started. Does your comparison count it, and should it?
A draft is published two days later. Is it in your denominator, and is it a success?

templates.title: Remix reach — distinct creators who duetted or stitched an original within 7 days
templates.subtopic: anti-join to find originals, as-of lookup of a setting, distinct counts per entity then summed, LEFT JOIN with conditions in ON

sections.scenario: Duets and stitches let creators build on each other's videos, and a creator can turn remixing off for a video. A creator-tools team wants a weekly measure of how far originals travel through remixes: for each original, how many different creators duetted or stitched it within 7 days of its publishing, summed over the originals published that week. Originals whose creator had remixing turned off when they were published are left out, because nobody could remix them. Settings change over time, so the current setting is not the one that applied.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns week_start, originals, remixed_originals, remix_creators, creators_per_original, one row per week with at least one counted original, ordered by week_start. An original is a video that does not appear in remixes as remix_video_id. It is counted if the setting in force at its published_at (the latest remix_settings row for it with changed_at at or before published_at) has remix_allowed = TRUE. Its reach is the number of distinct creators of remix videos whose source_video_id is the original, published at most 7 days (7 × 24 hours, exactly 7 days included) after it, not counting the original's own creator. Per week of the original's published_at (Monday 00:00 UTC; week_start is that Monday's date): originals counted, remixed_originals with reach above 0, remix_creators the sum of their reaches, and creators_per_original = remix_creators / originals rounded to 2 decimal places. {{setting_rule}} {{remix_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). The sample has {{videos}} videos, of which {{remixes}} are remixes. Every original has a setting row at or before its published_at.
sections.assumptions: Videos, creators, settings and the 7-day window are hypothetical; this exercise's rule, not a product definition (check current docs for how remix permissions work). Creator ids are opaque, and the measure describes videos in aggregate, never a person.
sections.criteria: Originals found with an anti-join; eligibility from the setting in force at publish time, not the latest (Hard+); distinct remix creators per original excluding the original's creator; the 7-day bound inclusive; zero-reach originals kept through a LEFT JOIN with conditions in ON; the original's week, not the remix's; remixes of remixes kept out (Very Hard); correct rounding and order; can discuss lineage roots and incremental computation.

clarifications.q: One creator made a duet and a stitch of the same original.
clarifications.a: One creator for that original.

clarifications.q: One creator remixed two different originals in the week.
clarifications.a: They count once for each original: reach is per original, then summed.

clarifications.q: The original's creator duetted their own video.
clarifications.a: Not counted.

clarifications.q: A remix published in the week after the original's week?
clarifications.a: It counts toward the original's week, if it is within 7 days.

clarifications.q: An original with remixing on and no remixes?
clarifications.a: It is counted in originals with reach 0.

hints: Find originals with NOT EXISTS against remixes.remix_video_id.
The setting in force at a time is the latest row at or before it: a correlated subquery with ORDER BY changed_at DESC LIMIT 1, or DISTINCT ON.
Compute reach per original with COUNT(DISTINCT …), then aggregate originals per week; a LEFT JOIN keeps originals with no remixes, if the filters live in the ON clause.
followups: The team also wants duets and stitches reported apart. A creator who did both: how do you count them in each column and in the total, and why do the columns no longer add up?
Turning remixing off after publishing does not delete existing remixes. Should a remix made just before the change count, and what does your query do?
Reach should also credit remixes of remixes to the root original (a stitch of a duet of it). How would you find the root, and how deep can chains go before a recursive query becomes the bottleneck?
At billions of videos, the as-of lookup per original and the distinct count per original are the expensive parts. How would you compute this incrementally each day?

rules.ask: A creator made a duet and a stitch of one original. What does your count give, and what is reach?
Distinct over the whole week, or per original? One creator remixed three originals this week: how many creators should the week show?
A creator turned remixing off a week after publishing. Which setting does your query read for that original, and which one does the rule want?
Your filter on the remix side is in WHERE after a LEFT JOIN. What happens to an original with no remixes in the window?
A remix lands exactly 7 days after its original. Is it in your reach?

templates.title: LIVE minutes and gifts per creator-day in the creator's time zone
templates.subtopic: local dates with AT TIME ZONE, splitting intervals at midnight with generate_series, anti-join exclusion, open intervals capped at a cutoff

sections.scenario: Creators who go LIVE see a daily summary of their own sessions: minutes live and the gifts viewers sent, valued in coins. Creators live in many time zones, so a "day" is the creator's local date, and LIVE sessions often run across local midnight: a session from 23:30 to 01:10 is 30 minutes on one day and 70 on the next, and a gift belongs to the local date it was sent. A gift can be reversed later (for this exercise, any reversal removes it from the summary; check current docs for how gift rules work). Viewers do not appear in the data.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns creator_id, local_date, live_minutes, gifts, coins, one row per creator and local date on which the creator was live for more than 0 minutes, ordered by creator_id, local_date. Local dates and times use the creator's time_zone. live_minutes is the total minutes of the creator's sessions that fall within that local date: a session that crosses local midnight is split there. gifts and coins count and sum the gifts sent during the creator's sessions whose sent_at falls on that local date, excluding every gift with at least one row in gift_reversals; a day without such gifts shows 0 and 0. The report runs at {{cutoff}} UTC. {{edge_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). The sample has {{sessions}} sessions and {{gifts}} gifts. Sessions start and end on whole minutes, one creator's sessions never overlap, and no daylight-saving change falls inside the data.
sections.assumptions: Creators, sessions, coin values and the reversal rule are hypothetical. The summary is shown only to the creator it describes; there is no information about who sent a gift.
sections.criteria: Local dates from the creator's time zone; sessions split at local midnight with no zero-minute rows; gifts dated by their own local send time; reversed gifts excluded once whatever the number of reversal rows (Hard+); half-hour zones handled (Hard+); open sessions counted to the cutoff (Very Hard); minutes and gifts aggregated separately and joined; correct order; can discuss time-zone moves, daylight-saving days and restatement after late reversals.

clarifications.q: A session runs 23:30 to 01:10 local.
clarifications.a: 30 minutes on the first date, 70 on the next.

clarifications.q: A session ends at exactly 00:00 local.
clarifications.a: Nothing on the next date, and no row for it unless another session is live then.

clarifications.q: A gift sent at 00:00:00 local?
clarifications.a: It belongs to the new date.

clarifications.q: A gift was reversed two days later. Does it count on the day it was sent?
clarifications.a: No. A reversed gift is excluded whenever it was reversed.

clarifications.q: Which time zone defines the date: the session's, the viewer's or UTC?
clarifications.a: The creator's, from creators.time_zone.

hints: ts AT TIME ZONE c.time_zone turns a timestamptz into the creator's local wall-clock time; its ::date is the local date.
For each session, generate_series(date_trunc('day', local_start), local_end, INTERVAL '1 day') lists the local dates it touches; each piece is LEAST(end, day + 1 day) − GREATEST(start, day).
Aggregate minutes and gifts separately and LEFT JOIN gifts onto the live days.
Very Hard: COALESCE(ended_at, <cutoff>) for sessions still live.
followups: A creator moves from one time zone to another mid-month. What should their history show, and what would you store to make it reproducible?
The data spans a daylight-saving change. What happens to a session across the change in your query, and is a "day" still 24 hours?
The creator also wants to see minutes and coins per session, with sessions across midnight shown whole. How do you serve both views from one model without double counting?
Gifts arrive as a stream of tens of thousands per second during big events, and reversals arrive days later. How would you keep the daily summary correct and restate it when a reversal lands?

rules.ask: In which time zone is that date taken? What does a session at 21:00 in Los Angeles get?
The whole session's length goes to one date. Where do the minutes after local midnight belong?
One gift has two reversal rows. What does your join do to the gift count and the coin sum?
AT TIME ZONE on a timestamptz gives a timestamp without zone. What does applying it a second time do, and where would that break?
A session is still live when the report runs. What does it contribute, and what changes when the report is re-run an hour later?

templates.title: Resumable upload assembly — fewest received byte ranges, or the first missing byte
templates.subtopic: sort once by start, furthest reach per step, first gap

sections.scenario: A long video is uploaded in parts, and on a phone that drops connections the client retries: a part is resent whole, resumed from the middle, or cut short when the network fails again. The server ends up with many overlapping byte ranges, some of them duplicates. Before the video can be processed, an assembler must decide whether every byte arrived and, if it did, which received ranges to read, as few as possible, so the file is stitched from the fewest reads. For a large file the server holds well over a hundred thousand ranges, and the assembler must answer quickly.
sections.problem: Implement assemble_upload(file_size, ranges). The file has bytes 0 … file_size − 1. Each range is (seq, first_byte, last_byte, checksum_ok): bytes first_byte to last_byte inclusive, received with the unique sequence number seq. Only ranges with checksum_ok True are usable. Assemble from byte 0: at each step, among the usable ranges that contain the first byte not yet covered, take the one whose last_byte is largest, breaking ties by the lowest seq; continue after its last byte. This rule picks the fewest ranges. Return ("complete", [seq, …]) with the chosen ranges in file order once the whole file is covered, or ("missing", offset) with the first byte that no usable range contains. {{order_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to 150 000 ranges and covers of more than 10 000 ranges. 0 ≤ first_byte ≤ last_byte < file_size and file_size ≥ 1. Rescanning every range at every step is O(n·k) for a cover of k ranges; aim for O(n log n).
sections.assumptions: File sizes, parts and sequence numbers are hypothetical. Nothing about the video's content is read or needed.
sections.criteria: A single sort by first byte and a forward sweep with a pointer, O(n log n); inclusive bounds and adjacency; the furthest end per step, ties by lowest seq; the first missing byte as the sentinel result, including 0; unordered input and duplicates (Hard+); failed checksums ignored and single-byte files (Very Hard); can prove the greedy and make it incremental.

clarifications.q: Two ranges [0, 199] and [200, 499]: is there a gap?
clarifications.a: No. Both ends are inclusive, so they meet.

clarifications.q: Two ranges end on the same byte. Which one?
clarifications.a: The lower seq, whatever their starts.

clarifications.q: What if no range starts at byte 0?
clarifications.a: Return ("missing", 0).

clarifications.q: May I sort the input?
clarifications.a: Yes; return the chosen seq values in file order.

clarifications.q: Can a failed range be used for bytes no other range has?
clarifications.a: No. A failed checksum means the bytes are not trusted; those bytes are missing.

hints: A range that starts after the first uncovered byte cannot help yet; a range that ends before it never will again.
Sort usable ranges by first_byte once. Keep a pointer: at each step, advance it over every range that starts at or before the uncovered byte, remembering the best end.
Each range is looked at once by the pointer, so the sweep is linear after the sort.
followups: Prove that taking the range that reaches furthest gives the fewest ranges.
The server must answer "is it complete yet?" after every received range, not once at the end. What would you keep so each arrival costs O(log n)?
Reads are cheaper when ranges are long and contiguous on disk. How would you change the objective to fewest bytes read twice, and is greedy still optimal?
Parts of one upload land on different servers. How would you assemble across them without moving every range to one place?

rules.ask: Your cover has 11 000 ranges and the server holds 132 000. How many range checks does your loop do in total?
What does each DP state depend on, and how many transitions are there for 132 000 ranges? Is there an exchange argument that removes the DP?
What does the heap order by, and what does it give you that a sorted list and one pointer do not?
Your ranges are inclusive. Where exactly does the next step start, and what does that do for two ranges that meet?
A failed range is the only one reaching furthest. Where in your loop is it filtered, and what is the first missing byte if it held a byte nobody else did?

templates.title: Comment thread display order with deleted comments kept as placeholders
templates.subtopic: children index, iterative pre-order DFS with an explicit stack, post-order pruning, sorted siblings

sections.scenario: Comments under a popular video become threads: replies to comments, replies to replies, and sometimes two people answering each other thousands of times. The display order is fixed for this exercise: replies sit under their parent, depth first, and siblings are ordered by a score you are given (highest first), then by id. A deleted comment that still has replies below it stays as a placeholder ("comment deleted") so the conversation keeps its shape; one with nothing left below it disappears. A thread export job lays out every comment of a video in this order, and the largest threads have a hundred thousand comments.
sections.problem: Implement thread_order(comments). Each comment is (comment_id, parent_id, score, deleted); parent_id is None for a top-level comment. Return a list of (comment_id, depth, placeholder) in display order: top-level comments at depth 0 ordered by score descending, then comment_id ascending; after each comment, its replies (depth + 1) in the same order, each followed by its own replies, depth first. A comment that is not deleted is always shown with placeholder False. A deleted comment is shown with placeholder True if at least one comment below it (at any depth) is shown, and is left out with everything below it otherwise. {{input_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to 100 000 comments in one thread, and reply chains can be tens of thousands deep. Scanning all comments for each comment's replies is O(n²). Recursion stops at Python's default recursion limit (1 000). Aim for O(n log n) without recursion.
sections.assumptions: Comment ids, scores and threads are hypothetical. The score is input data; how it is computed is out of scope, as is anything a comment says. No information about who wrote a comment is used.
sections.criteria: A children index built once and siblings sorted once; an iterative depth-first walk with correct depths; deleted comments shown as placeholders exactly when something below is shown, decided without recursion; ties by id; unordered input and purged parents shown at the top level (Very Hard); O(n log n) and no recursion limit; can discuss paging, changing scores and partitioned threads.

clarifications.q: Two replies have the same score.
clarifications.a: The lower comment_id first.

clarifications.q: A deleted comment whose only reply was also deleted?
clarifications.a: Both disappear.

clarifications.q: A deleted comment above a deleted reply above a live reply?
clarifications.a: Both deleted comments are shown as placeholders.

clarifications.q: Is depth counted from 0?
clarifications.a: Yes. A top-level comment is depth 0, its replies depth 1.

clarifications.q: Can parent links form a cycle?
clarifications.a: No.

hints: Build a dict from parent id to its replies once, and sort each list of siblings once.
Replace recursion with a stack of (comment_id, depth): push a comment's replies in reverse order so the first one is popped next.
Whether a deleted comment is shown depends on what is below it. The reverse of a pre-order visits every reply before its parent, so one backward pass decides it.
followups: Viewers load threads page by page: the first 20 top-level comments with up to 3 replies each, then "view more". How would you serve that without laying out the whole thread?
Scores change constantly. How would you keep the order stable while someone is reading, and when do you re-sort?
A comment is deleted while the export runs. What guarantees does your output give, and what would you snapshot?
Threads of the largest videos are stored across many partitions by comment id. How would you build the display order without loading the thread onto one machine?

rules.ask: A reply chain is 20 000 deep. What happens to your function at depth 1 000, and is raising the recursion limit a fix you would ship?
That works on this machine. What decides the real stack depth, and what happens in a runtime with a smaller stack?
For each of 100 000 comments you scan every comment for its replies. How many checks is that?
How do you know a deleted comment has a live reply three levels down before you print the deleted comment?
How many times does your code sort, and over what? Is it once per sibling list or once per visit?

templates.title: Remix lineage — the nearest video two remixes share
templates.subtopic: lowest common ancestor by binary lifting over a forest of duets and stitches

sections.scenario: A duet or a stitch is made from one earlier video, its source, and that source may itself be a duet or stitch of something older. Trends grow into long chains: each creator stitches the previous creator's video, and side branches split off along the way. An analytics job answers questions about pairs of videos taken from trend reports: do these two videos belong to the same remix family, and if so, which video is the nearest one they both descend from? That shared video is where the two branches of the trend split. The job receives the remix log and many pairs at once.
sections.problem: Implement common_origin(remixes, pairs, deleted=frozenset()). remixes is a list of (video, source) rows: video was made as a duet or stitch of source. Each video has at most one source, rows are in no particular order, and the lineage never loops. A video that is never the first element of a row is an original. A video is known if it appears in at least one row, as either element. pairs is a list of (a, b) pairs of video ids. A video descends from itself, from its source, from its source's source, and so on. For each pair, return the nearest video that both a and b descend from — the one furthest from the original — or None if they share none. If one video of the pair descends from the other, the answer is the other one; a video paired with itself is itself. Return one answer per pair, in the order of pairs. {{data_rule}} {{deleted_rule}}
sections.constraints: The timing check has up to 4 remix chains 15 000 videos deep with tens of thousands of side branches (about 90 000 videos) and 15 000 pairs. Walking up both videos' chains for every pair costs tens of thousands of steps per pair, over 10⁸ in total, and is too slow. Something close to O((n + q) log n) is expected. Do not rely on recursion: chains are far deeper than Python's recursion limit.
sections.assumptions: Video ids, chains and pair lists are hypothetical; how deep a real trend goes, and what counts as a remix, are this exercise's rules (check current docs). The remix log is already validated: no video has two sources and there are no cycles. The job uses only the lineage, never who made or watched the videos.
sections.criteria: Correct answers when one video descends from the other, for a video paired with itself, for siblings and for cousins at different depths; None for separate families and unknown ids; repeated rows harmless; at Very Hard, deleted videos kept in the lineage but never returned, including a deleted video in the pair itself; no recursion on deep chains; an index built once, with binary lifting, an Euler tour with range minimum, or offline Tarjan, rather than a walk per pair; a clear complexity argument; sensible answers on incremental updates and distributed computation.

clarifications.q: Does the kind of remix matter, duet or stitch?
clarifications.a: No. Both make the new video a remix of its source, and both count the same.

clarifications.q: If b is a remix of a remix of a, what is the answer?
clarifications.a: a. a descends from itself, and b descends from a.

clarifications.q: Two videos are in different remix families.
clarifications.a: They share no video, so the answer is None.

clarifications.q: Are the rows sorted so that a source comes before its remixes?
clarifications.a: No. Build whatever index you need first.

clarifications.q: Can I answer each pair on its own?
clarifications.a: You can, but the pairs arrive together, and the chains are deep. Spend time once on an index so that each pair is cheap.

hints: Give every video an integer index, its source's index and its depth (the number of remix steps from its original). Compute depths without recursion, for example by walking up to the first video whose depth is already known and filling the path on the way back.
For two videos in the same family, first lift the deeper one until both are at the same depth. If they are now the same video, that is the answer.

Keep, for each video, its 2ᵏ-th source for every k (up[k][v] = up[k-1][up[k-1][v]]). Lifting by any distance then takes O(log n) jumps, and so does finding the last depth at which the two chains still differ.
followups: The trend report also wants, for each pair, how many remix steps separate the two videos through their shared video. What do you add, and what does it cost?
New remixes arrive all day, and pairs are asked as they come. Which part of your index can be extended for a new video without rebuilding, and why?
A creator deletes a video in the middle of a chain. Its remixes stay up. Should the answer ever be a deleted video, and what changes in your index if it may not be?
The remix log has two billion rows and does not fit on one machine. How would you compute the nearest shared video for a batch of a million pairs in a distributed job?

rules.ask: A trend chain is 15 000 stitches deep and you have 15 000 pairs. How many steps does your loop take, and what would you precompute to avoid it?
The deepest chain is 15 000 videos long. What happens to your recursive function in CPython, and how do you rewrite it?
How much memory does your table take for 90 000 videos, and how do you choose how many levels to build?
That works too. How do you build the Euler tour without recursion, and how does its memory compare with binary lifting?
Offline answers are fine for this batch job. What changes if pairs start arriving one at a time from a live dashboard?

templates.title: Sound match — aligning a clip's fingerprint with a sound library
templates.subtopic: inverted index of fingerprint hashes and voting on alignment offsets

sections.scenario: When a creator uploads a video with audio, the service checks whether the audio is a clip of a sound in its library, so the video can link to that sound's page and follow its regional licence. A fingerprinter you are given turns audio into one integer hash per short frame. A library sound is a long list of frame hashes, and the uploaded clip is a shorter list. The clip is noisy: talking, room sound and compression change many of its frames, so only some hashes match. The question is where the clip lines up best: in which sound, starting at which frame, with how many matching frames.
sections.problem: Implement best_alignment(library, clip, min_votes=1, max_repeat=None). library maps a sound id to its list of integer hashes, one per frame. clip is a list of hashes, one per frame. An alignment places the whole clip inside one sound starting at frame offset, where 0 ≤ offset ≤ len(sound) − len(clip); a clip longer than a sound has no alignment in it. The alignment's votes are the number of clip positions i with clip[i] == sound[offset + i]. Return (sound_id, offset, votes) for the alignment with the most votes; on a tie, the smaller sound id, then the smaller offset. Return None if the best alignment has fewer than min_votes votes (so, with min_votes = 1, when no frame matches anywhere). {{gap_rule}} {{repeat_rule}}
sections.constraints: The timing check has up to 400 sounds of 1 000 to 7 000 frames each, about 1.5 million frames in all, and a clip of 1 500 frames. Hashes are spread over a range of about 16 million values, so most clip hashes occur in only a few places. Trying every offset in every sound is O(n·m), about 2 × 10⁹ comparisons. Finding each clip hash's positions by scanning the sounds is also O(n·m), even when the scan runs in C. Something close to O(n + m + matches) is expected.
sections.assumptions: Sounds, hashes and the fingerprinter are hypothetical; this exercise does not say how any real audio matching works, and the rules for linking a clip to a sound are this exercise's (check current docs). The fingerprinter is a black box. The clip is not stretched or sped up: frame i of the clip lines up with frame offset + i of the sound. Nothing about the uploader is used.
sections.criteria: Votes counted per offset with each clip position voting once; only offsets where the whole clip fits; ties to the smaller sound id, then the smaller offset; None below min_votes and when nothing matches; at Hard and above, None frames keep their positions and never vote, and the threshold is inclusive; at Very Hard, a hash occurring more than max_repeat times in a sound casts no votes in that sound only; an index of hashes with offset voting rather than a scan per offset or per hash; a clear complexity argument in terms of matches; sensible answers on library-scale indexing and stretched clips.

clarifications.q: Can the clip hang over the end of a sound?
clarifications.a: No. Only offsets where the whole clip fits count, so an offset whose clip frames would run past the end gets no votes.

clarifications.q: A hash appears three times in the clip and four times in the sound. How many votes is that?
clarifications.a: Count per offset: each clip position votes at most once for a given offset, when the sound has the same hash at offset + i.

clarifications.q: How are sound ids compared on a tie?
clarifications.a: As strings, in ordinary lexicographic order.

clarifications.q: Should I return the alignment with the best ratio of votes to clip length?
clarifications.a: No. Most votes, then the tie rules. The clip length is the same for every alignment.

clarifications.q: Can I load the library into a dictionary first?
clarifications.a: Yes. Whatever index you build counts towards the time.

hints: A match between clip position i and sound position p votes for exactly one alignment: offset = p − i. You never need to look at an offset that no match votes for.
Index one side by hash. Indexing the clip (hash → clip positions) and scanning each sound once finds every match in O(n + matches).
Count votes per offset in a dictionary for each sound, discard offsets outside 0 … len(sound) − len(clip), and keep the best by (−votes, sound_id, offset).
followups: The library grows to a hundred million sounds. You cannot scan it per upload. What do you index ahead of time, and how big is it?
Clips are sometimes sped up by a few per cent, so offsets drift along the clip. How would you change the vote so that a stretched clip still matches?
Two different sounds share a sample, so a clip matches both with similar votes. How would you decide which sound to link, or whether to link none?
The check runs at upload time for every video. What latency budget would you set, and what do you do with uploads whose check times out?

rules.ask: There are 1.5 million offsets and 1 500 clip frames. How many comparisons is that, and which offsets could you skip without looking?
That scan runs in C. How many elements does it touch for one clip of 1 500 hashes against 1.5 million library frames?
Which side do you index, the clip or the library, and how does that choice change for one upload against a fixed library versus a batch of uploads?
Two alignments tie on votes. Show how your code picks the smaller sound id and offset, and test it.
You drop the None frames before you start. What happens to the offsets of the frames after them?

templates.title: Debug the regional sound availability check
templates.subtopic: exclusive end dates, region groups, local midnight, lapsed versus never licensed, renewals

sections.scenario: A sound can be used in videos only where and while a licence covers it. Licences name countries and region groups, with a start date and an end date in each country's local calendar. When a licence lapses in a country, videos that already use the sound keep playing there without it (muted); a sound that has never been licensed in a country cannot be used there at all (blocked). Creators and the music partnerships team have reported several problems with the check that decides this. A sound shows as available for a whole extra day after its licence ends. Sounds licensed for a region group are blocked in every country of the group. In Japan a sound becomes available nine hours after the licence starts. A sound announced for next month shows as muted, as if it had been withdrawn. A sound whose licence was renewed after a gap shows as muted for the whole of its first licence period. The check below is the suspect.
sections.problem:
Fix sound_status(licences, groups, offsets, checks) so that it meets this specification. {{replay_rule}}

  1. licences are dicts {"sound", "regions", "start", "end"}. regions is a list of country codes and region-group names. start and end are dates "YYYY-MM-DD" in each country's local calendar: a licence covers a country from 00:00 local time on start up to, but not including, 00:00 local time on end. end is None for a licence with no end date. A sound can have several licences in one country: a renewal can start on the day the previous licence ends, or after a gap.
  2. groups maps a region-group name to its list of country codes. Group names never equal a country code, and groups never contain other groups. A country named directly and through a group is covered once.
  3. offsets maps every country code to its fixed UTC offset in minutes, positive east of UTC (for example 540 for UTC+9 and −360 for UTC−6).
  4. checks is a list of (sound, country, ts) with ts in Unix seconds (UTC).
  5. Output. One status per check, in order: "available" if a licence for the sound covers the country at ts; otherwise "muted" if a licence for the sound covered the country at some earlier moment (it has lapsed); otherwise "blocked" (never licensed there up to ts, including a sound whose only licence there starts later).
sections.constraints: Keep the function's name, arguments and output format. Up to 200 000 checks against 20 000 sounds, processed in close to linear time.
sections.assumptions: Offsets are fixed for this exercise, with no daylight-saving changes. Sounds, licences, groups and dates are hypothetical, and the muted and blocked behaviour is this exercise's rule (check current docs for how any real licensing works). Licences are already validated: a licence's start is before its end.
sections.criteria: Finds and explains every bug with its creator-facing symptom; end dates exclusive; region groups expanded to their countries; licence boundaries at each country's local midnight with the right sign; blocked rather than muted for a sound licensed only in the future; renewals kept alongside earlier licences, with the gap muted; minimal, linear fixes that keep the output format; a regression test per bug.

clarifications.q: Is the end date covered?
clarifications.a: No. The end date is the first local day the licence no longer covers.

clarifications.q: Whose midnight starts a licence in a region group?
clarifications.a: Each country's own: the same licence starts at different UTC moments in Tokyo and in Mexico City.

clarifications.q: What if a sound's licence starts next month and someone checks today?
clarifications.a: It has never been licensed there yet, so it is blocked. Muted is only for a licence that has lapsed.

clarifications.q: Does a renewal replace the earlier licence?
clarifications.a: No. Both periods count. A check during the first period is available, a check in the gap between them is muted.

clarifications.q: How many bugs are there?
clarifications.a: Several, of different kinds. The checks point at each one.

hints: Work out the UTC moment at which a licence starting on 2026-04-01 begins in a country at UTC+9, then compare with what _midnight returns.
Read the line that computes end. What does the comment say, and what does the specification say?
Follow a licence for ["NORDICS"] through _countries and into windows.
Put two licences for the same sound and country into windows by hand. What is left?
followups: Countries change their UTC offset for daylight saving. What would you store instead of a fixed offset, and how do you compute local midnight on the day the clocks change?
The check runs for every video play. How would you precompute licence windows so that a play costs one lookup, and what invalidates your cache when a licence is amended?
A sound's licence lapses in one country. Which videos must be muted, and how would you produce that list and the hours each kept playing after the lapse?
The music partnerships team wants a history: for any past date, the status of a sound in every country, as the licences were known then (before later corrections). What do you add to the data model?

rules.ask: A licence starts on 1 April in Tokyo and in Mexico City. At which UTC moments does it start in each, and what does your code compute?
With named time zones, local midnight can fall in a skipped hour on some days. How would you define the start of the licence then?
Your licence covers up to the end date. Show the check at noon on the end date and say which status it should get.
A sound has fifty renewals in one country. How do you find whether any covers a moment, and would sorting the windows help?
A licence is signed today for next month. What do creators in that country see today, and what would they see if the check said muted?

templates.title: Captions and translations — versions, requests and what each viewer was shown
templates.subtopic: auto-captions, creator edits, on-demand translation, serving logs joined to versions

sections.scenario: About {{daily_uploads}} videos with speech are uploaded a day. Each gets auto-captions in its spoken language from a speech model you are given. The creator can review and edit the captions, and edits are most common within {{edit_window}} of posting. Viewers can ask for a translation into any of {{languages}} supported languages, and translations are produced on request by a translation model you are given, then reused. Models are upgraded every few weeks. The quality team wants to know which caption version each viewer was shown, so that a complaint about a wrong caption can be traced to the exact text, model and edit, and so that the share of views shown creator-edited captions can be reported by language and week.
sections.problem: Design the data and pipeline for captions and translations. Cover the caption version as an entity (what identifies it, what it is derived from), creator edits and their effect on existing translations, translation on request with reuse and deduplication of concurrent requests, model upgrades and whether old captions are regenerated, what the player logs when it shows captions, how a view is joined to the exact version shown, retention of {{retention}} for serving logs, and the aggregates the quality team reads.
sections.constraints: A creator's edit must reach viewers within minutes. Translations must never be served for an older caption version without saying so in the logs. Two viewers asking for the same translation at the same moment must not trigger two model runs. Serving logs carry no viewer identifier beyond what the aggregate needs. Reports are by language pair, model version and week, and they must be re-runnable.
sections.assumptions: Volumes, the language count, the edit window and retention are hypothetical; how any real caption or translation feature behaves is not described here, so check current docs. The speech and translation models are black boxes with version ids. Captions are a list of timed cues. Nothing about the speaker or the viewer is inferred from captions.
sections.criteria: Immutable caption versions with lineage (source, model, parent version, language); a current-version pointer per video and language; edits that mark or regenerate dependent translations explicitly; on-request translation with a cache keyed by source version and target language and deduplication of concurrent requests; a stated policy for model upgrades that never overwrites creator edits; player logs that carry the version id; aggregates by language pair, model and week, re-runnable; no viewer profiles; retention enforced; a plan for each incident.

clarifications.q: Does an edit create a new version or change the old one?
clarifications.a: That is part of your design, but the quality team must be able to see exactly what was shown before the edit.

clarifications.q: When the creator edits the original captions, what happens to existing translations?
clarifications.a: Decide. They were made from the old text; you must say whether they are regenerated, marked stale or served as they are.

clarifications.q: Are all {{languages}} translations produced at upload?
clarifications.a: No. Only on request, then reused for later viewers.

clarifications.q: Do we regenerate every caption when the speech model is upgraded?
clarifications.a: Not necessarily. Weigh cost against quality and say what you would do for edited captions.

clarifications.q: Can the quality team see which viewer saw which caption?
clarifications.a: No. They see versions and aggregates; a complaint carries the video, the language and the time.

hints: Make a caption version immutable and identify it by what it was derived from: the video, the source (auto or creator edit), the model version, and for a translation, the source caption version and the target language.
Keep a pointer per video and language to the current version, so an edit or a regeneration is a new version plus a pointer swap.
Have the player log the version id it rendered, not just the language, so every view joins to exactly one version.
followups: A creator edits captions twenty times in an hour. How many translation runs do you allow, and what do viewers in other languages see meanwhile?
A new speech model is better for most languages but worse for one. How would you roll it out by language and measure it with the serving logs?
A creator deletes their video. What happens to its caption versions, translations, cached files and serving logs?
At {{daily_uploads}} uploads a day, translation requests spike for a video that goes viral in a new country. How do you keep the model from being overwhelmed while still serving something?

rules.ask: A viewer complains about a caption shown yesterday, and the creator has edited it since. Where is the text the viewer saw?
What is the cache key for a translation, and what happens to the cached file when the source caption changes?
How much would regenerating every caption for a model upgrade cost at {{daily_uploads}} uploads a day, and which ones would you skip?
Two requests for the same translation arrive within a millisecond on different servers. Walk through what happens.
Which report needs that identifier? Could the aggregate be computed without it?

incidents: A translation cache keyed by video and language serves translations of an outdated caption for {{edit_window}} after creator edits, and complaints rise in one language.
A model upgrade regenerates auto-captions, overwrites creator-edited ones for a day, and creators report their corrections were lost.
Serving logs past {{retention}} are not deleted for one region because a partition naming change broke the deletion job.

templates.title: Effects usage from the in-app editor, reported to effect makers in aggregate
templates.subtopic: versioned catalogue entities, device capability checks, failed renders, aggregate reporting with suppression

sections.scenario: The in-app editor offers about {{effects}} effects, many made by independent effect makers, and each effect is published in versions. There are about {{daily_sessions}} editor sessions a day. When a creator opens an effect, the app first checks whether the device can run it (for example GPU features, memory, camera); then the effect renders in preview, may be applied to a recording, and the video may be posted. Renders sometimes fail or fall back to a simpler mode. Phones queue events offline for up to {{offline_hours}} hours. Effect makers want a daily report for their own effects: opens, devices that could not run it, failed renders by effect version and device class, recordings and posted videos. They must see aggregates only, and never anything about an individual creator or device.
sections.problem: Design the pipeline from editor events to the effect makers' reports. Cover the event model (open, capability check, preview render, failure or fallback, apply, record, post) and how one effect use is identified across them, effect versions and how events are tied to the version actually rendered, device classes and how capability results are recorded, late and duplicate events from offline phones, the report tables, suppression of cells under {{min_cell}}, and how a maker sees only their own effects.
sections.constraints: A failed render must be attributed to the effect version that failed, not to the version currently published. Device information is reduced to a coarse class before it reaches any maker-facing table. Cells with fewer than {{min_cell}} sessions are suppressed in a way that cannot be undone by subtracting from totals. Reports for a day may change for {{offline_hours}} hours and then become final. No creator id reaches the maker's report.
sections.assumptions: Volumes, effect counts, the suppression threshold and the offline window are hypothetical; how any real editor or effect platform works is not described here, so check current docs. A device class is a coarse bucket (for example by chipset tier and OS major version) defined by the platform. Effects are hosted by the platform and identified by effect id and version.
sections.criteria: An event model with a per-use id that joins open, check, render, apply, record and post; failures tied to the loaded version and package hash; capability failures and fallbacks reported apart from failed renders; device details reduced to classes at ingestion; late and duplicate events handled with a bounded deduplication window and days finalised after {{offline_hours}} hours; maker tables keyed by effect and scoped to the maker's own effects; suppression under {{min_cell}} that is protected against subtraction; no creator identifiers in maker reports; a plan for each incident.

clarifications.q: An effect is updated while a creator is mid-session with the old version. Which version do events belong to?
clarifications.a: The version that was actually loaded and rendered on the device.

clarifications.q: Do capability-check failures count as failed renders?
clarifications.a: No. A device that cannot run the effect never renders it; report those apart.

clarifications.q: Does a fallback to a simpler mode count as a failure?
clarifications.a: Report it as its own outcome, because the effect did render, but not as designed.

clarifications.q: Can a maker see which creators used their effect?
clarifications.a: No. Makers see aggregates by day, version, device class and country group, with small cells suppressed.

clarifications.q: What links a post to the effect?
clarifications.a: That is part of your design; the posted video should record the effect id and version it used.

hints: Give each effect use a client-minted id when the effect is opened, and carry it on every later event of that use, so funnels join without a creator id.
Put the effect version and a content hash of the downloaded package on every render event, so a failure is tied to what actually ran.
Reduce device details to a class on the server at ingestion, and build maker tables only from the reduced events.
followups: A maker publishes a version that crashes on one device class. How quickly can your pipeline show it, and could the platform pull the version automatically?
A maker has one niche effect used in fewer than {{min_cell}} sessions a day. What can they see, and how would you let them see weekly totals without breaking suppression?
The platform wants a ranking of effects for the editor's browse page. What would you keep out of that ranking's input from this pipeline, and why?
At {{daily_sessions}} sessions a day, the deduplication of offline events dominates cost. How would you bound it?

rules.ask: Which maker report needs that level of detail? What do you reduce it to before any maker-facing table, and where does the reduction happen?
A maker sees a total and every cell but one. How do you stop them from working out the suppressed cell?
Version 7 was published at noon; a creator's phone ran version 6 at 12:05 and failed. Where does your pipeline put that failure?
Offline phones send the same render event twice after {{offline_hours}} hours. Where is the duplicate dropped, and for how long do you remember ids?
A failure rate jumps from 0.5% to 4% for one version and device class. Is that enough sessions to alert on, and what would you show the maker?

incidents: An app release logs the currently published effect version instead of the loaded one, and a fixed effect keeps showing failures for {{offline_hours}} hours of late events.
A maker notices that a cell suppressed under {{min_cell}} can be recovered by subtracting the other device classes from the daily total.
A new device class is added server-side, and its events are dropped from reports for three days because the class mapping did not know it.

templates.title: Videos as data — drafts, uploads and processing states, visibility settings, caption edits after posting, and a video as it stood on a date
templates.subtopic: lifecycle states as events, effective-dated settings, versioned captions, deletion as a state, as-of reconstruction

sections.scenario: Creators publish about {{uploads_per_day}} videos a day. A video starts as a draft in the in-app editor; in this exercise a draft saved to the account is kept for {{draft_days}} days (this exercise's rule). When the creator posts, the upload can be interrupted and resumed, then the video is processed (transcoded, checked, captioned) and becomes published, or processing fails and the creator is asked to retry. After posting, the creator can change who can watch it (everyone, friends only, only me), change its caption text and cover, turn comments, duets and stitches on or off, and delete it. There are about {{setting_changes_per_day}} such setting changes a day. A video can also be restricted or removed by a moderation decision, which this model records as an outcome only. Creator analytics, support and transparency reporting all need the same answer to "what was this video's state, visibility and caption on date D?", for up to {{history_years}} years.
sections.problem: Design the data model for videos across their life. Cover the video's identity and owner; drafts and their expiry; upload attempts and resumptions; processing states and failures; publishing; visibility and interaction settings as effective-dated records; caption and cover versions; moderation outcomes as a state that refers to a decision kept elsewhere; deletion by the creator. Show the queries for "the video as it stood at time T" (state, visibility, caption version, interaction settings) and for "per day, how many videos were publicly visible", and say which tables are facts, which are dimensions, and at what grain.
sections.constraints: Nothing is overwritten: each change is a new record with an event time and a recorded time, and clients send changes late after being offline. A video has exactly one owner. Visibility applies from the instant it changes. A deleted video keeps no caption text or media after this exercise's retention period, but the fact that a video existed and when it was deleted stays for counting. Viewer data is out of scope; creator-facing numbers about a video are shown only to its owner. Moderation outcomes are recorded by decision id and policy area code only.
sections.assumptions: Volumes, the draft period and the history window are hypothetical. Media storage and transcoding internals are out of scope: model their outcomes, not their mechanics. Account-level privacy settings exist; assume a video's visibility is its own setting, defaulted from the account at posting time.
sections.criteria: Identity, lifecycle events, settings and content versions kept apart, all append-only with event and recorded times; drafts excluded from published metrics and expired; visibility derived from video and account settings in force at T; "as of T" and "per day" queries that are precise about intervals; deletion that removes content after retention while keeping counts reproducible; moderation outcomes by decision id only; owner-only creator data; sizing of intervals versus snapshots; incidents explained and repaired from the stored events.

clarifications.q: Is a draft a video?
clarifications.a: Your choice, but drafts that are never posted must not count as videos in any published metric, and they expire after {{draft_days}} days.

clarifications.q: Can a published video go back to processing?
clarifications.a: Yes: in this exercise replacing the cover or re-captioning does not, but a media replacement after a failed check does. Say how you represent a video that is published but temporarily unavailable.

clarifications.q: If the account becomes private, does every video become friends-only?
clarifications.a: In this exercise the account setting changes who can see the account's videos without editing each video's own setting; the effective visibility is derived from both.

clarifications.q: What does "the video on date D" mean when a change arrived late?
clarifications.a: Two answers: what was true on D, and what the system showed on D. Say which each consumer needs.

clarifications.q: Can a creator undo a deletion?
clarifications.a: No, in this exercise deletion is final.

hints: Separate the lifecycle (draft, uploading, processing, published, unavailable, deleted) from the settings (visibility, interactions) and from the content versions (caption, cover); each changes on its own clock.
Settings as effective-dated rows make "state at T" a lookup of the row in force at T per setting; the account setting is a second effective-dated input to the derived visibility.
Event time and recorded time differ for offline edits; keep both.
followups: Write the query for "publicly visible videos per day" that treats a video made private at 14:00 correctly. Visible at any moment of the day, at the end of the day, or for a share of the day: which do you choose and why?
A creator changed a caption offline at 09:00 and the change reached the server at 11:00. What did a viewer see at 10:00, and what does your "as of 10:00" query return?
A creator deletes a video. Which rows are kept, which are erased, and how do the per-day counts for earlier days stay unchanged?

At {{uploads_per_day}} uploads a day over {{history_years}} years, would you keep a daily snapshot of every video's state, or intervals? Estimate the rows and the cost of the "as of T" query for each.
Processing fails for 1% of uploads, and creators retry with a new upload. Is the retry the same video or a new one, and how does each choice change the upload success metric?

rules.ask: A support agent asks what state the video was in yesterday at 15:00, before a failed reprocess. With one status column updated in place, how do you answer?
The account became private for two hours last week while the video stayed "everyone". Was the video public in those hours, and where does your model say so?
An offline caption edit arrives two hours late. Your valid-from is the edit's time. How do you answer what viewers were shown in those two hours?
After this exercise's retention period the caption text must be gone. Which columns does your soft delete leave behind, and how do last month's counts still include the video?
How many rows is that per day at {{uploads_per_day}} uploads a day for {{history_years}} years, and what happens to the snapshot when a late edit lands?

incidents: After a client release, visibility changes were recorded with the device's local time instead of UTC. For about {{setting_changes_per_day}} changes that day, "made private at" times are off by hours, and the daily count of publicly visible videos moved by several percent in two regions.
A resumed upload produced a second "published" event for the same video. Upload success per day counted the video twice, and the creator's video count showed one more video than they had.
A history query for {{history_years}} years of settings timed out when support looked up one video, because the settings table was partitioned by change date and the query had no date bound.

templates.title: Remix lineage as data — duets and stitches, the clip range taken, each original's remix permissions over time, and attribution as of a date
templates.subtopic: typed edges between videos, permissions in force at creation time, chains of remixes, attribution that survives deletion and renames

sections.scenario: Creators remix each other's videos about {{remixes_per_day}} times a day. A duet places the new video beside the original for its length; a stitch takes a clip of up to {{stitch_limit}} from the original and plays it before the new video (this exercise's rule; check current docs). A remix can itself be remixed, so chains form; the longest chains in the data are about {{max_depth}} remixes deep. Each original's creator chooses whether duets and stitches are allowed and for whom (everyone, friends, no one), and changes it about {{permission_changes_per_day}} times a day across all videos. A remix shows an attribution to the original's creator. Creators ask "who remixed my video, and when"; the support team asks "was this remix allowed when it was made"; creator analytics show per original how many remixes it drew.
sections.problem: Design the data model for remix lineage. Cover the remix as a typed link between two videos (duet or stitch), the clip range taken for a stitch, the permission settings of each original over time, the permission in force when each remix was created and the check's outcome, the chain from any remix back to its root original, and the attribution shown on a remix as of a date. Show the queries for: remixes of one original per week by type; all descendants of an original; the root of a given remix; and "was this remix allowed when it was created".
sections.constraints: A remix's parent never changes once posted. Permissions are effective-dated, and a later change does not retroactively invalidate an earlier remix (this exercise's rule). If the original is deleted or made private, the remix stays up in this exercise but its attribution shows that the original is unavailable; the link stays in the data for counting. Creator handles can change; attribution must follow the account, not the handle text. Remix counts shown to a creator cover only their own originals, and never list a remix that is not visible to them.
sections.assumptions: Volumes, the stitch limit and the depth are hypothetical. Sounds reused by remixes are modelled elsewhere. Videos and their visibility are modelled as in a separate video model; refer to it by id.
sections.criteria: Remix as a typed edge on the child with clip range; effective-dated permissions per original and the outcome of the check stored at creation; no retroactive invalidation; attribution by account id, resolved to a handle as of a date; deletion and visibility handled without losing counts or exposing hidden remixes; a sized choice among recursion, a stored root and depth, and a closure table; owner-scoped lists and aggregate-only analytics; incidents explained and repaired from stored data.

clarifications.q: Can a stitch take a clip from a remix rather than an original?
clarifications.a: Yes. The "original" of a remix is its direct parent; the root is the first video of the chain.

clarifications.q: What if the clip range is longer than {{stitch_limit}}?
clarifications.a: The editor prevents it, but the data occasionally contains one from an old client version. Say what your model does with it.

clarifications.q: When a creator turns stitches off, what happens to existing stitches?
clarifications.a: Nothing, in this exercise: they stay. New stitches are refused from that instant.

clarifications.q: Is "who remixed my video" a list of accounts?
clarifications.a: For the creator of the original, yes, limited to remixes they are allowed to see; any wider analytics use counts only.

clarifications.q: Does a remix have one parent?
clarifications.a: Yes, exactly one.

hints: A remix is an edge with a type and attributes (clip start and end for a stitch), stored on the child video because each child has exactly one parent.
Permissions are an effective-dated table per original; the check at creation is a lookup of the row in force at the remix's creation time, worth storing with its outcome.
For descendants and roots, compare a recursive query, a stored root id and depth on each remix, and a closure table; size each against {{max_depth}} and {{remixes_per_day}}.
followups: Write the query "remixes of original V per week by type", counting only remixes created while the corresponding permission allowed them. Where does that rule come from in your tables?
The original's creator changed their handle twice since a stitch was posted. What does the stitch show today, and what did it show last month?
Store the root id on every remix, or compute it on read? What happens to your choice when a video in the middle of a chain is deleted?
A closure table for chains up to {{max_depth}} deep at {{remixes_per_day}} remixes a day: how many rows a day in the worst case, and when is it worth it?

Support asks why a duet was allowed although duets were off. The permission change and the duet were recorded within the same second. What decides it, and what do you store so it can be explained later?

rules.ask: The parent is deleted. What does your parent column point to, and do the original's weekly remix counts change?
A chain is {{max_depth}} remixes deep and support needs the root in under a second for many remixes at once. What do you store so you do not recurse on every request?
How many closure rows does one new remix at depth {{max_depth}} add, and how do you keep the table consistent when the remix and its closure rows are written separately?
A single "allowed" column on the video is overwritten when the creator changes it. How do you tell whether a remix made last week was allowed at the time?
Handles change and can be reused by another account later. What does attribution store, and what does it show after a handle is reused?

incidents: After an editor release, stitches arrived with clip ranges measured in frames instead of milliseconds. About a day of the {{remixes_per_day}} remixes shows clips far longer than {{stitch_limit}}, and a validation job flagged them all as violations.

A permission lookup used the original's current setting instead of the setting in force at creation. When a popular creator turned duets off, a report listed thousands of earlier duets as "not allowed", and support began to answer complaints from it.
A descendant-count job that recursed through chains up to {{max_depth}} deep ran out of memory on one viral original, and the original's creator saw a remix count of zero for a day.

templates.title: Sounds as data — original sounds and licensed tracks, regional licence windows, the clips videos use, and videos muted when a licence lapses
templates.subtopic: sounds of two origins, licences per territory as half-open windows, clip usage per video, per-region mute decisions with a trail

sections.scenario: Videos use sounds. Some are original sounds: the audio of a creator's own video, which other creators can reuse. Others are licensed tracks from a music catalogue, which in this exercise may be used only in the regions and during the windows a licence covers (this exercise's model; check current docs). There are about {{sounds}} sounds, of which about {{licensed_tracks}} are licensed tracks, across {{regions}} regions. A video uses a clip of a sound: an offset into it, a duration and a volume mix with the creator's own audio. When a track's licence ends in a region without a renewal, every video using it must be muted in that region; in this exercise a mute is permanent, and the creator can replace the sound. A single licence ending can affect about {{lapse_videos}} videos. Sound pages show how many videos use a sound; the rights team asks what was licensed where on a date; creators ask why their video is silent in one region.
sections.problem: Design the data model for sounds and their use. Cover original sounds (who created them, from which video) and licensed tracks (catalogue id, rights holder ids); the link when an original sound is identified as containing a licensed track; licences per track and region as time windows, including renewals and region groups; the clip each video uses; and per-region mute decisions with their reason and time. Show the queries for: "where could track X be used at time T"; "which videos must be muted when this licence ends"; and "the number of videos using a sound per region and day, counting a muted video as no longer using it".
sections.constraints: Licence windows are half-open: a licence allows use from its start up to but not including its end. A licence can be granted for a region group, which this model must expand to regions as of the grant. Mutes are per video and region, with a reason, the licence they enforce, and the time they took effect. An original sound found to contain a licensed track keeps its identity and gains a link; the link has its own effective time. Sound pages show counts only; the list of videos using a sound shows only videos visible to the viewer.
sections.assumptions: Counts are hypothetical. Audio fingerprinting is out of scope: assume an identification feed that says which original sounds contain which tracks, with a confidence you are given. Royalty accounting is out of scope.
sections.criteria: Sounds of both origins with identity kept, licensed tracks and identification links with effective times; licences as half-open windows per region, region groups expanded at grant time; lapse defined as an uncovered end, renewals at the exact end handled; clips per video; mutes as per-region decisions with reason, licence and time; counts that honour mutes and replacements; creator-only detail; incidents traced to the model and repaired, including how permanent mutes made by mistake are reviewed and reversed through a recorded correction.

clarifications.q: Does a renewal that starts exactly when the old licence ends cause a lapse?
clarifications.a: No. With half-open windows, a renewal starting at the old end covers that instant.

clarifications.q: Can a muted video get its sound back?
clarifications.a: Not in this exercise; the creator can replace the sound, which is a new clip record.

clarifications.q: Are region groups stable?
clarifications.a: No: a group can gain or lose a region. A licence covers the regions the group had when it was granted, in this exercise.

clarifications.q: What if two licences for the same track and region overlap?
clarifications.a: That is allowed; the track is licensed while any of them covers the instant.

clarifications.q: Who sees why a video was muted?
clarifications.a: Its creator, with the reason category and the date; no one else sees per-video detail.

hints: Keep the sound (identity) apart from the licence (permission over time and place) and from the clip (one video's use of one sound).
"Is X licensed in R at T" is an interval test: any licence with start ≤ T < end. A lapse is an end that no licence of the same track and region covers.
A mute is a decision with a reason that refers to a licence; store it as a row, not as a flag on the video.
followups: Write the query that lists the videos to mute when licence L ends at time E, excluding videos already muted in that region and handling a renewal that starts exactly at E.
A region group that the licence named gains a region a month after the grant. Is the track licensed in the new region? Where does your model answer that?
An original sound is identified as containing a licensed track not licensed in five regions. Which videos are affected, and what do the creators see?
With {{lapse_videos}} videos to mute at one instant, how do you produce and apply the mute decisions without falling hours behind, and how would you measure the lag?
Sound pages show "videos using this sound" per region. How do you keep that count correct across mutes and replacements without recounting every day?

rules.ask: A track's licence ends in 12 regions next Friday and is renewed in 9 of them, one starting an hour late. Where does a flag store that, and what does it say at 00:30 on Saturday?
A creator asks why their video is silent in one region since Tuesday. Which licence, which reason and which time does your flag give you?
The old licence ends at midnight and the renewal starts at midnight. With BETWEEN on both ends, is that instant covered twice, and which videos does your lapse query mute?
The group gained a region after the grant. Does your expansion run at grant time or at query time, and which did this exercise's rule ask for?
A muted video replaces its sound with another. Which sound's count changes, in which regions, and from what time?

incidents: A renewal for one track was loaded with its start an hour after the old licence's end because of a time zone error. In that hour the lapse job muted about {{lapse_videos}} videos in one region; with permanent mutes, the creators' videos stayed silent although the track was licensed again.

A region group used by many licences was edited to add a region, and a query that expanded groups at read time showed the tracks as licensed there since the original grants. A rights report for the quarter was wrong across {{regions}} regions.
Sound-page counts in one region stayed high after a lapse: the count was maintained by a counter that was decremented when a video was deleted but not when it was muted.

templates.title: Comments and reports as data — threads and replies, creator filters, reports, moderation decisions and appeals, as a process
templates.subtopic: threaded comments, filter outcomes with versions, reports grouped into cases, decisions and appeals with policy versions, aggregate-only reporting

sections.scenario: Viewers post about {{comments_per_day}} comments a day on videos, in {{languages}} languages; a comment can be a reply to another comment. Creators can turn on filters for their own videos: a filter list they maintain and a default filter for comments a score you are given marks as likely to break the rules. A filtered comment is held: it is visible to its author and, for review, to the creator, but not to others. Anyone can report a comment under a policy area; there are about {{reports_per_day}} reports a day. Reports about the same comment are grouped into one case that is reviewed; the decision is no action, restrict, or remove, under a versioned policy. The comment's author can appeal a decision within {{appeal_days}} days (this exercise's rule; check current docs), and an appeal can overturn it. Transparency reporting publishes aggregate counts of decisions by policy area and region.
sections.problem: Design the data model for comments and the moderation process around them. Cover comments and replies with their thread; deletion by the author; creator filter settings and filter lists as versions; filter outcomes per comment; reports and their grouping into cases; review decisions with the policy version and the decision's effect on visibility; appeals and their outcomes; and the visible state of a comment as of a time. Show the queries for: "the visible thread under a video at time T for a viewer"; "per policy area, region and week, cases decided, removed, and removed then reinstated on appeal"; and "time from first report to decision" per queue.
sections.constraints: No comment text appears in any analytics table; analytics carry ids, policy area codes and counts only. The identity of a reporter is never shown to the reported author or to the creator. The author sees their own comment's state and any decision about it, with the policy area. Reviewer identifiers stay in the operational system; analytics do not carry them and no reviewer is ranked. A decision is never edited: an appeal outcome is a new decision that supersedes it. A deleted comment's text is erased after this exercise's retention period; its replies remain and the thread shows a placeholder.
sections.assumptions: Volumes, the appeal window and the language count are hypothetical. Queue routing and reviewer tooling are out of scope beyond the fields this model needs. The score you are given is produced elsewhere and is stored with its version.
sections.criteria: Threaded comments with deletion and placeholders; filter settings and lists versioned with the version recorded per outcome; reports grouped into one open case per comment with a concurrency guard; decisions append-only with policy versions, appeals superseding them; visible state at T derived from independent inputs; analytics free of text, reporter and reviewer identifiers; reproducible weekly counts with a stated restatement rule and small-cell protection; incidents explained and repaired; moderation described only as process.

clarifications.q: Do several reports on one comment create several cases?
clarifications.a: No. Reports open one case per comment while it is open; a report after the decision opens a new case only if the comment is still visible.

clarifications.q: Can the creator see who reported?
clarifications.a: No. The creator sees held comments on their own videos and can approve or delete them; reporter identity is never shown.

clarifications.q: When a filter list changes, are earlier comments re-filtered?
clarifications.a: Not in this exercise: a filter applies from the version in force when the comment was posted. Say how you record which version applied.

clarifications.q: Does a removed parent hide its replies?
clarifications.a: No; the thread shows a placeholder for the parent and keeps its visible replies.

clarifications.q: What counts as "reinstated"?
clarifications.a: A removal superseded by an appeal decision of no action.

hints: A comment's visible state is derived from several independent inputs: author deletion, filter outcome, creator approval, and the latest decision. Store each as its own record.
Reports are many-to-one with a case; decisions belong to cases, and an appeal is a case of its own that refers to the decision it challenges.
Weekly transparency counts must be reproducible after appeals: decide whether a week's numbers are restated when an appeal lands later, and record the policy version used.
followups: Write the query for the visible thread at time T, with placeholders for removed or deleted parents that have visible replies.
A filter list version changes at 12:00. A comment posted at 11:59 arrives at 12:01 from a client that was offline. Which version applies, and where is that recorded?
A removal is overturned on appeal 20 days later. Which weekly counts change: the week of the removal, the week of the appeal, or both? How do you publish a restatement?
At {{reports_per_day}} reports a day, how do you group reports into open cases without two cases being opened for the same comment by concurrent reports?
The transparency report shows a policy area with three removals in a small region. What do you publish, and what rule protects the people involved?

rules.ask: A comment was filtered, approved by the creator, then removed after a report, then reinstated on appeal. What does a single status say, and how do you rebuild what a viewer saw at 14:00 yesterday?
A coordinated burst sends 5,000 reports about one comment. How many cases does your model open, and what does "reports per day" in the transparency report mean then?
An appeal overturns a removal. With the decision overwritten, how do you count removals for the week they happened, and how do you show the author the history?
Analytics never carry reviewer ids and nobody is ranked. Which grain do your queue metrics use, and how do you keep those ids out of the warehouse?
Which tables hold the text, how long, and what removes it after the author deletes the comment? Show that no analytics table needs it.
