incidents: Concurrent reports on a widely shared comment opened 40 cases for it within a minute. Reviewers handled the same comment repeatedly, and the weekly "cases decided" for that policy area was overstated in the transparency draft.

Appeals overturned a batch of removals {{appeal_days}} days later, but the weekly transparency counts were computed once and never restated; published removals and reinstatements no longer added up for those weeks.

After a filter list editor bug, held comments were recorded without the filter version that applied. Creators asked why comments were held, and the support team could not tell which version of their list had held them.

templates.title: Lapsed sounds — videos still playing a sound after its licence ended in their region, and hours until muted
templates.subtopic: half-open licence windows, uncovered ends, earliest of several stop times, permanent mutes, FILTER aggregates

sections.scenario: In this exercise's model a licensed track (a sound with kind = 'licensed') may be used in a region only while a licence covers that instant (check current docs for how real music licensing works). When a licence ends without a renewal, every video using the sound must be muted in that region by a mute job, which writes a row to video_mutes. The rights team wants a monthly readout per region: how many videos were still playing a sound after its licence had ended, how many of those lapses ended with a mute, how long the mutes took, and how many are still playing now. The sample's regions are {{regions}}, and the data is a snapshot taken at {{as_of}}.
sections.problem:
Write one PostgreSQL query that returns region, lapse_month, video_lapses, muted, still_playing, avg_hours_to_mute, max_hours_to_mute, one row per region and lapse month with at least one video lapse, ordered by region, then lapse_month.

  • A licence allows its sound in its region from licence_start (inclusive) up to licence_end (exclusive). A licence whose licence_end is after {{as_of}} has not ended yet and is ignored.
  • {{renewal_rule}}
  • A video lapses at a licence end when it uses that licence's sound, was published before the end (published_at < licence_end), and was not muted in that region at or before the end. Mutes are per region and permanent: the video's earliest row in video_mutes for that region is when it was muted. One video can lapse in several regions. Original sounds have no licence rows and never lapse.
  • {{removal_rule}}
  • A lapse ends at the earliest of the events this statement names (at least the video's first mute in that region after the end). It counts in muted when that earliest event is the mute (a mute that coincides with another event counts as the mute), and in still_playing when nothing has ended it by {{as_of}}. A lapse that ends any other way counts only in video_lapses.
  • lapse_month is the licence end's month in UTC as text, YYYY-MM. video_lapses counts lapses (a video and a licence end). avg_hours_to_mute and max_hours_to_mute are the hours from the licence end to the mute over the lapses counted in muted, each rounded to 1 decimal; NULL when muted is 0.
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). All timestamps are TIMESTAMPTZ and the session time zone is UTC. Use ROUND(numeric, 1). Do not use now(): the snapshot time is {{as_of}}. The sample has {{licence_count}} licences, {{video_count}} videos and {{mute_rows}} mute rows; production has hundreds of millions of videos using licensed sounds and a readout due every morning.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical schema, sounds, regions and times; this is not how any real licensing or muting system works. Every timestamp in the sample other than some licence ends is at or before {{as_of}}.
sections.criteria: Lapses built from licence ends at or before the snapshot that no licence covers (half-open windows, renewals at the exact end handled); earliest mute per video and region with a LEFT JOIN; published-before and removed-at-or-before filters at the end instant; the lapse's end as the earliest of the stated events, with a mute winning a tie; counts with FILTER and hours over muted lapses only, from exact intervals, rounded once; deterministic order; can discuss alerting, region groups, precomputation at scale and restoration on renewal.

clarifications.q: A video was muted at exactly licence_end. Is that a lapse?
clarifications.a: No. The sound may play up to but not including licence_end; a mute at that instant is on time.

clarifications.q: Should a video muted before the licence ended appear?
clarifications.a: No. It was not playing the sound when the licence ended.

clarifications.q: Does lapse_month follow the mute or the licence end?
clarifications.a: The licence end, in UTC.

clarifications.q: Can one video lapse twice in the same region?
clarifications.a: At the hardest level, yes, after a renewal; each lapse counts once in video_lapses.

clarifications.q: If a sound's licence is renewed, does a muted video get its sound back?
clarifications.a: No; mutes are permanent in this exercise.

hints: Build the lapses first: licence ends at or before {{as_of}} that no licence of the same sound and region covers.
Reduce video_mutes to the earliest mute per video and region before joining, then LEFT JOIN it: a video that was never muted must stay.
LEAST ignores NULLs, so the earliest of several possible end events is one expression; COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE …) and AVG(…) FILTER (WHERE …) keep the whole readout in one GROUP BY.
followups: The mute job is expected to finish within 2 hours of a licence end. Change the query into an alert that lists every region and licence with lapses still playing after 2 hours, as of {{as_of}}.
Licences are now granted to region groups that change over time. What changes in the schema and in your lapse definition?
In production a popular sound is used by tens of millions of videos. How would you avoid joining every video to every licence end each morning, and what would you precompute?
The rights team decides that a renewed licence restores the sound to muted videos. Which rows would represent that, and how would "still playing" and the hours change?

rules.ask: The mute job retries and can write a second row hours later. Which of the rows is the moment the video went silent, and what does the latest one do to your hours?
A video that was never muted has no row in video_mutes. Where does it go in your query, and which column should it have counted in?
Why would now() make this readout differ between two runs on the same data, and what makes it reproducible?
One video lapsed twice in one region and month after a renewal. What does COUNT(DISTINCT video_id) report, and what did the statement ask you to count?
Is a licence's end instant inside the licence? Show what your comparison does with a renewal that starts exactly at the old end.

incidents: At month end many licences ended at the same instant and the mute job fell behind; in one region thousands of lapses stayed in still_playing for over a day. A dashboard that showed only the average hours of muted lapses looked normal throughout, because still-playing lapses are not in it.

A renewal was loaded with its licence_start one hour after the old licence_end because of a time zone error. The readout showed a one-hour lapse for every video using the sound in that region, and the mute job, seeing the gap, muted them all permanently.

templates.title: Comment moderation queues at scale — reports, priorities by language, SLAs, appeals and reviewer well-being
templates.subtopic: report deduplication, priority queues by language, SLAs, appeals, exposure limits

sections.scenario: People post {{comments_per_day}} comments a day on videos and LIVE sessions, in {{languages}} languages. Anyone can report a comment, and reports arrive at {{reports_per_day}} a day; one comment can be reported by many people within minutes. A separate system gives each comment a priority score (a score you are given, with a version); you do not design it. Trained reviewers, each qualified in one or more languages, decide whether a reported comment stays up, is removed, or is limited, under a versioned set of community guidelines. The person who posted it, and the creator whose video it was posted on, can appeal a decision. In this exercise's rules, every report is decided within {{sla_hours}} hours, an appeal is decided by a different reviewer, and no reviewer handles more than {{exposure_cap}} cases a shift that the score marks as high severity.
sections.problem: Design the moderation workflow system: intake of reports and scores; how many reports about one comment become one case; queues by language and priority, and how cases are routed to qualified reviewers; the SLA clock and what happens as it nears; decisions as records that every surface (the video page, LIVE, notifications, search) applies; appeals; and the reviewer experience, including how the exposure cap and breaks are enforced by the system rather than left to each reviewer. Describe the process only; you never need an example of content.
sections.constraints: A removed comment disappears from every surface within one minute of the decision. Each case is decided by someone qualified in its language. Every decision records who decided, under which guidelines version and which score version, and can be audited years later. Reporters are never shown to the reported person. Reviewer well-being is a requirement, not a preference: exposure caps, breaks and the option to step away from a case are enforced by the tooling.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, SLAs, caps and staffing figures are hypothetical, and the guidelines, appeal and SLA rules are this exercise's rules (check current docs). Reviewers work in shifts across several time zones. The score arrives within seconds of a comment or a report, and is sometimes missing.
sections.criteria: Reports, cases and decisions as separate records with deduplication into one case per comment and open period; per-language queues with an ordering that combines priority and SLA age, overflow to qualified reviewers in other regions, and explicit handling of undetermined languages; decisions as an append-only, versioned log that every surface consumes with a freshness check; appeals routed away from the original reviewer by construction; exposure caps, breaks and stepping away enforced by the assignment step, with well-being measures that never rank individuals; score and guidelines versions recorded on every decision; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Does every report need a human decision?
clarifications.a: In this exercise, yes, every case gets a human decision; the score sets only priority and the queue. Say what you would change if some cases could be decided automatically, and what that would need.

clarifications.q: What if a comment's language cannot be determined?
clarifications.a: It goes to a queue for undetermined language with reviewers who can triage and re-route it. Say how that queue avoids becoming a dumping ground.

clarifications.q: Can a comment be reported again after a decision to keep it?
clarifications.a: Yes. Decide when new reports reopen a case and when they are attached to the closed case.

clarifications.q: Is the SLA from the first report or the latest?
clarifications.a: From the first report that created the case.

clarifications.q: Can reviewers see who reported?
clarifications.a: They see how many reports a case has and their timing, not who made them.

hints: Separate reports (many, noisy, deduplicated) from cases (one per comment and open period) from decisions (append-only, versioned). Every surface consumes decisions, never reports.
A priority queue per language is simple until one language floods. Think about how priority, SLA age and reviewer capacity combine into the order cases are offered.
The exposure cap is a property of the assignment step: the system decides what a reviewer is offered next, so it can count, pause and rotate.
followups: Walk one comment from its first report to a removal that every surface honours. Which records change, and where can a decision be lost?
How do you order work within a language queue when high-priority cases are fresh but low-priority cases are near their {{sla_hours}}-hour deadline?
One language's reports jump tenfold for a day while its reviewers are asleep. What does the system do automatically, and what needs a person?
How do you measure decision quality and consistency across {{languages}} languages without turning it into a ranking of individual reviewers?
The guidelines change on a date. What happens to open cases, to appeals of decisions made under the old version, and to the audit trail?

rules.ask: Thirty people report the same comment within two minutes. How many cases does your queue hold, and how do you keep it at one?
High-priority cases arrive all day. Under your ordering, how long does a low-priority case wait, and does it ever breach the SLA?
The score's new version is wrong for one language for six hours. What has your automation done by the time anyone notices, and how do you undo it?
Which of those measures could push reviewers to work past the exposure cap or skip breaks, and how does your design prevent that?
An appeal arrives a month later. What does the second reviewer look at, and who else can see it?

incidents: A creator with a very large following is LIVE, and reports in one of the {{languages}} languages rise forty times in an hour. That language's queue passes {{sla_hours}} hours while queues for other languages are nearly empty.

The score you are given moves to a new version overnight. The share of cases marked high severity doubles, reviewers reach the {{exposure_cap}}-case cap two hours into their shift, and high-severity cases stop being assigned.
A decision service deploy writes removals to the case store but not to the stream the surfaces read. For three hours, removed comments still show on videos and in LIVE.
An audit finds 4% of appeals were decided by the reviewer who made the original decision, after a routing change that grouped work by language and time zone.

templates.title: LIVE gifting at scale — coins, gifts, on-screen totals, creator rewards and reversals
templates.subtopic: balances, hot keys, approximate live totals over an exact ledger, reversals

sections.scenario: Viewers buy coins with money through the app's purchase channels and spend them on virtual gifts during a creator's LIVE session. At peak there are {{concurrent_lives}} LIVE sessions at once and {{peak_gifts}} gifts sent per second across all of them; during a big event one session receives {{top_live_share}} of all gifts. Each gift shows on screen, and the session shows a running gift total. In this exercise's rules, gifts a creator receives are converted into creator rewards at a stated rate, rewards stay pending for {{hold_days}} days, and a coin purchase that is refunded or charged back within {{reversal_days}} days reverses the rewards from gifts paid with those coins.
sections.problem: Design the gifting system: coin purchases and coin balances; sending a gift during a LIVE; the on-screen gift animation and running totals; the creator's rewards, from pending to available; reversals after a purchase is refunded or charged back; and the creator-facing statement of gifts and rewards per session and per day. Say what must be exact, what may be approximate, and how one very busy session is handled.
sections.constraints: A viewer can never spend more coins than they hold, even with several devices sending at once. A gift appears on screen within one second of sending. A creator's statement must match the gifts recorded, gift by gift, after every reversal. Coins and rewards are whole units; any conversion to money is in integer minor units and rounds once, by this exercise's rule. Viewers appear to a creator only as the gifts they chose to send in that creator's session; nothing else about a viewer is shown or inferred.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, rates, hold and reversal windows are hypothetical; the conversion and programme rules are this exercise's rules (check current docs). Purchase confirmations, refunds and chargebacks arrive from the purchase channels as events, sometimes days late and occasionally twice.
sections.criteria: Identifies the per-viewer coin balance as the exact, contended-only-by-one-person boundary and the creator's totals as aggregated, lagging projections; an append-only ledger with idempotency keys from the client for gifts and from the channel for purchase events; conditional balance debits that cannot overspend across devices; a hot-session strategy (sharded or pre-aggregated totals, batched fan-out of on-screen events) isolated from other sessions; holds, reversals with a stated coin-matching rule, and negative adjustments shown clearly to creators; whole units and integer minor units with one rounding step; month-end reconciliation across purchases, spends, rewards and reversals; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Can a viewer send gifts from two devices at once?
clarifications.a: Yes, and both may be offline briefly. Neither may overspend.

clarifications.q: Which coins does a reversal take back if a viewer bought coins several times?
clarifications.a: Your choice, stated as a rule (for example, coins spent first-in-first-out against purchases). Be ready to explain a statement under it.

clarifications.q: What if the reversed coins were already spent and the creator's rewards already paid out?
clarifications.a: This exercise's rule: rewards still pending are reversed; rewards already paid become a negative adjustment on the creator's next statement. Say what the creator sees.

clarifications.q: Must the running total on screen be exact?
clarifications.a: It must never go down except for a stated reason and must agree with the statement within a minute after the session ends.

hints: Find the consistency boundary. The coin balance is per viewer and contended only by that viewer's devices; the creator's totals are contended by everyone in the session but can lag.
Make the ledger append-only: purchases, gifts, conversions, holds, releases, reversals, each with an id that makes a retry harmless.
On-screen totals and statements are projections of the ledger. One is fast and approximate, the other exact and slower.
followups: Walk one gift from the tap to the creator's statement. Which records are written synchronously, and which later?
The busiest session receives {{top_live_share}} of {{peak_gifts}} gifts per second. Where does that load land in your design, and what stops it hurting every other session?
A purchase is charged back on day {{reversal_days}}, after the coins funded gifts in four creators' sessions. Show the ledger entries and what each creator's statement shows.
How do you prove at month end that coins sold, coins spent, rewards created, reversed and paid all reconcile?
A region's purchase channel goes down for an hour during a big event. Do viewers keep gifting with coins they already hold, and what can go wrong when it returns?

rules.ask: The node holding the busiest session's running total restarts. What does the screen show next, and how do you rebuild it?
Which two records are in your transaction, and does the creator's side really need to be in it at {{peak_gifts}} gifts per second?
A gift request times out on a phone and is sent again. What key makes the second one harmless, and who generates it?
Where is the only place a fraction of a minor unit can appear in your design, and how is it rounded?
A creator's next statement is negative after reversals. What does the creator see, and how do you explain each line?

incidents: During a big event the busiest session receives {{top_live_share}} of all gifts. The partition holding its running total falls behind by four minutes, and the on-screen total freezes while gifts keep animating.
A purchase channel resends a day of refund events. Without deduplication, pending rewards (held for {{hold_days}} days) of thousands of creators are reversed twice.
A deploy lets two devices of one viewer both pass the balance check within the same 50 ms; some viewers end the hour with negative coin balances.
Chargebacks for one purchase channel arrive {{reversal_days}} days late in a single batch, and rewards already paid out must be adjusted on creators' next statements.

templates.title: Screen-time and well-being settings honoured on every device
templates.subtopic: versioned settings with precedence, cross-device usage totals, offline enforcement

sections.scenario: {{accounts}} accounts use the app on phones, tablets, web browsers and TV apps, with up to {{devices}} devices signed in to one account. Screen-time and well-being settings include a daily screen-time limit, reminders to take a break, a reminder at a chosen time each evening, and a time window when notifications are muted. In this exercise's rules, accounts whose declared age is under 18 start with a daily limit of {{default_minutes}} minutes and stricter defaults, set by declared age band; the account holder may change some of them, and a parent-linked account (described generally) may set and lock others. When the limit is reached, the app asks for a passcode to keep watching. Devices report usage time every {{sync_seconds}} seconds when online and can be offline for up to {{offline_hours}} hours.
sections.problem: Design the system that stores these settings, applies the defaults for an account's declared age band, resolves who may change what, syncs settings to every device, adds up usage time across devices into a daily total, and enforces the limit and reminders on every device, online or offline. Cover the settings model and its versions, the precedence rules, the usage-time pipeline, the day boundary, enforcement on the device, and the audit of who changed what. Say what a parent-linked account can and cannot see.
sections.constraints: A locked setting changed by a parent-linked account reaches every online device within one minute, and an offline device applies it on reconnection before anything else. The daily total counts each second of use once, even when two devices play at the same time. Usage data is kept only as daily totals per account after this exercise's retention period, and never includes which videos were watched. A parent-linked account sees settings and daily totals, not viewing history, messages or comments.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, defaults, age bands and timings are hypothetical, and the defaults and parent-linking rules are this exercise's rules (check current docs). The declared age is the age on the account; how it was collected or verified is out of scope. An account has one home time zone, which the account holder can change.
sections.criteria: Settings as versioned values with source, lock and precedence rules, not last write wins by device clock; defaults derived from declared age band with scheduled band transitions that keep explicit choices; a settings sync that applies locked changes first on reconnection; usage as intervals per device, deduplicated and unioned per account day in the home time zone; device-side enforcement with a stated offline policy; minimal usage data with retention limits and no viewing history; parent-linked visibility limited to settings and totals; an audit log of every change; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Is "a day" the device's local day or the account's?
clarifications.a: The account's home time zone, in this exercise. Say what a traveller sees and what happens on the day the home time zone changes.

clarifications.q: If two devices play at once, does that count as double time?
clarifications.a: No. Screen time is the union of the intervals when any device was in use.

clarifications.q: What happens when a declared age band changes, for example on a birthday?
clarifications.a: The defaults for the new band apply from that local date; settings the account holder or a parent-linked account chose explicitly are kept unless this exercise's rules for the new band forbid them. Say how you schedule it.

clarifications.q: Can the account holder turn off a setting a parent-linked account locked?
clarifications.a: No. They can see that it is locked and by whom.

clarifications.q: Does enforcement happen on the server or the device?
clarifications.a: Both are possible; the device must enforce while offline.

hints: Store each setting as a value with a source (default, account holder, parent-linked account), a lock flag and a version; the effective value comes from a precedence rule, not from whichever write arrived last.
Usage time is a set of intervals per device. A daily total is the length of their union in the account's day, which tolerates late and overlapping reports.
Offline, a device knows the server's last total plus its own unsent intervals. Decide whether it errs towards stopping early or late, and say why.
followups: Walk a parent-linked account lowering a locked daily limit while the teen is watching on a TV that is offline. What does each device do, and when?
How do you compute the daily total from {{devices}} devices whose reports arrive late, overlap and repeat?
A device has been offline for {{offline_hours}} hours. What limit does it enforce, and what happens when its usage arrives and the account is already over?
A declared age band changes at local midnight for a few million accounts on the same day. How do you apply new defaults without a thundering herd?
How would you show, a year later, exactly which settings were in effect on a given day and who set them?

rules.ask: A parent-linked account locks a limit, then a teen's offline tablet syncs an older change to the same setting. Which value wins under your rule, and is that right?
A phone and a TV both play for the same twenty minutes. How many minutes does your total show?
The device is offline when the locked setting changes. What does it do when it comes back, before anything else?
An account's home time zone is eight hours from UTC. When does its day reset under your design, and what does the account holder see?
Which usage fields leave the device, how long are they kept, and who can read them?

incidents: A settings-sync release makes devices apply the newest write by device clock. A teen's tablet with a clock set ahead overrides a parent-linked lock on {{devices}} devices for two days.
A usage-ingest backlog delays reports by three hours. Devices that rely on the server total let accounts run well past their {{default_minutes}}-minute limit, and the evening reminder fires late.
The daily total is computed as a sum of per-device minutes instead of a union. Accounts that cast to a TV while the phone stays open reach their limit in half the time, and support contacts spike.

Daylight-saving time ends in one region; accounts there get a 25-hour day, and the limit resets an hour early for some devices and an hour late for others because devices and server disagree on the day boundary.

templates.title: Creator rewards programme — eligibility, qualified views, daily estimates, restatements and statements
templates.subtopic: eligibility as of a date, qualified-view counting, provisional vs final, restatements

sections.scenario: A creator rewards programme pays eligible creators for qualified views of their videos. In this exercise's rules, a creator is eligible on a date if their declared age is 18 or over, they have at least {{min_followers}} followers, their account is in good standing, and they live in a region where the programme is offered; a view is qualified if it lasts at least {{min_seconds}} seconds, on a video at least one minute long, posted while the creator was eligible, and is not later found to be invalid activity. Invalid activity is identified by a separate process (a list of view ids and a reason, delivered up to {{review_days}} days after the views). Rewards are a rate per 1,000 qualified views that varies by region and is restated monthly. {{creators}} creators are enrolled, and their videos receive {{daily_views}} views a day.
sections.problem: Design the rewards system: eligibility as of each date; counting qualified views from view events; the daily estimate a creator sees the next morning; the monthly statement that becomes final after the {{review_days}}-day review; restatements when invalid activity, a late eligibility change or a rate correction arrives; and the creator-facing statements and their explanations. Say what a creator can see about their viewers (aggregates only) and what is never shown.
sections.constraints: The daily estimate is available by 09:00 in the creator's time zone. A final statement never changes; a later correction is a dated adjustment on a later statement, with its reason. Every amount on a statement can be traced to counts by video, day and region. Amounts are integer minor units, rounded once per statement line by this exercise's rule. A creator sees counts of qualified views and rewards for their own videos; nothing identifies an individual viewer or infers anything about viewers' traits.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, thresholds, windows and rates are hypothetical, and the eligibility, qualification and payment rules are this exercise's rules (check current docs). View events arrive within hours, occasionally days late from offline devices. The invalid-activity process is a given; you do not design it and do not need to know how it works.
sections.criteria: Eligibility as dated intervals with backdated corrections, and video eligibility fixed at posting; deduplicated view events counted at the grain of video, date and viewer region with provisional and invalid counts separated; estimates computed incrementally per creator time zone and labelled as estimates; final statements as immutable snapshots with later corrections as dated adjustments with reasons; integer minor units with one rounding step per line; full traceability from amount to counts; viewer data shown only as aggregates with nothing inferred; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: If a creator drops below {{min_followers}} followers mid-month, do earlier views still count?
clarifications.a: Yes. Eligibility is evaluated per date; views on dates when the creator was eligible count.

clarifications.q: Does a video posted before the creator became eligible ever earn?
clarifications.a: Not in this exercise's rules. Say how you store that.

clarifications.q: Is the daily estimate a promise?
clarifications.a: No. It is labelled an estimate; the final number may be lower after review. Say how you show the difference.

clarifications.q: Which region's rate applies: the creator's or the viewer's?
clarifications.a: The viewer's region in this exercise, aggregated so no individual viewer is identifiable.

clarifications.q: What if invalid activity is found after the statement is final?
clarifications.a: A negative adjustment on the next statement, with the reason and the affected month.

hints: Treat eligibility as intervals per creator and a video's eligibility as fixed at posting; joining views to those intervals is an as-of question.
Keep counts at the grain of (video, view date, viewer region) with provisional and invalid counts separate. Estimates, statements and adjustments are all derived from that table.
A final statement is a snapshot. Corrections land in the next open period, never in the closed one.
followups: Walk one view from the event to a line on a final statement. Which tables change, and when does the line stop changing?
How do you produce estimates for {{creators}} creators by 09:00 in every time zone without recomputing all of history daily?
Invalid activity for 3% of one day's views arrives on day {{review_days}}, after the month closed. Show what each affected creator sees, and how you keep totals consistent.
The region rate for last month was wrong by 2% for one region. How do you restate, and how do you explain it to creators?
A creator disputes a statement. What evidence can you show them, and what can you never show?

rules.ask: You recompute last month after the statement is final. What happens to the number the creator was already paid against?
A creator's account standing changes, then is reversed on appeal a week later, backdated. How do your eligibility intervals record that?
An offline device uploads the same views twice, three days late. Which day do they count on, and how many times?
Estimates are 20% higher than finals for one region every month. What do you change, and what do you tell creators?
What exactly does a creator see about the people who watched, and what stops it identifying anyone?

incidents: The invalid-activity list for one week arrives {{review_days}} days late, after statements were finalised. About 4% of qualified views in one region are removed, and thousands of creators get negative adjustments on their next statement.
A change to the view pipeline counts views shorter than {{min_seconds}} seconds for two days. Daily estimates jump 30% and then drop back, and creators open support tickets about the drop.
The eligibility job runs before a backdated standing reversal is recorded. A few thousand creators show no earnings for a week of dates they were eligible on.
Estimates for creators in a time zone far east of UTC are ready at 14:00 local time, because the daily job waits for the UTC day to close.

templates.title: Transparency reporting — moderation actions by policy area and region, restated after appeals, small cells suppressed
templates.subtopic: counts from a decision ledger, versioned taxonomies, restatement, small-cell suppression

sections.scenario: Every quarter the service publishes a transparency report: counts of moderation actions on videos, comments and accounts, by policy area, region and quarter, with how many were appealed and how many were restored after appeal, as tables and downloadable data files. Moderation decisions are recorded as they are made, about {{decisions_per_quarter}} a quarter, across {{regions}} regions and {{policy_areas}} policy areas. The policy areas are revised from time to time. In this exercise's rules, an appeal can be filed within {{appeal_days}} days of a decision, and any published cell with fewer than {{min_cell}} actions is suppressed.
sections.problem: Design the reporting system: the decision ledger it reads from; exact definitions of each published count; how a quarter's numbers are frozen and published; how later appeals and corrections restate earlier quarters; how policy areas that change between quarters are compared; how small cells are suppressed so that no suppressed number can be worked out from the totals; and how the published files, the tables and internal dashboards are shown to agree.
sections.constraints: Every published number is reproducible from the ledger as of the report's cut-off date and is traceable to the decisions it counts. A published report never changes silently: restatements appear in the next report, marked, with the old and new values. Suppressed cells cannot be recovered by subtracting the published cells from a published total. Nothing published concerns an individual person, video or comment; the report contains only counts.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, regions, policy areas and thresholds are hypothetical, and the appeal window, suppression and publication rules are this exercise's rules (check current docs). A decision's region is the region of the account that posted the content, as recorded at decision time. Decisions can be reversed by appeal or by a later review, and both are events in the ledger.
sections.criteria: An append-only decision ledger with reversal events and as-of cut-offs so every report can be rerun; precise definitions of each count, including the quarter a restoration falls in; frozen quarterly snapshots with restatements published as marked old and new values in the next report; versioned policy-area mappings that handle splits from decision-level data; region recorded at decision time; complementary suppression across rows, columns and totals (or a stated alternative such as publishing ranges) with a check that suppressed cells cannot be recovered; one computation feeding files, tables and dashboards with reconciliation; only counts published; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Is an action counted in the quarter it was taken or the quarter of the content?
clarifications.a: The quarter of the decision, by its UTC timestamp, in this exercise.

clarifications.q: If a decision is restored on appeal, is it still counted as an action?
clarifications.a: It counts as an action in its quarter and as restored in the quarter the appeal was decided. Say how you present both.

clarifications.q: Does a decision that is later moved to another policy area move between rows?
clarifications.a: In this exercise it is restated in the next report, under its final policy area, with a note.

clarifications.q: Are automated and human decisions shown separately?
clarifications.a: Yes, as two columns; each decision records which it was.

clarifications.q: Who checks the report before publication?
clarifications.a: A review step with sign-off; your system should make the review easy and the numbers reproducible.

hints: Count from an append-only ledger with as-of semantics: the report for a quarter is a query over the ledger as of a cut-off timestamp, so it can always be rerun.
Map old policy areas to new ones with an explicit, versioned mapping; some old areas split, and a split cannot be reversed without the decision-level data.
Suppressing one cell in a row whose total is published reveals it by subtraction. Suppression has to consider rows, columns and totals together.
followups: Define "actions restored after appeal" precisely. Which quarter does each restoration fall in, and why?
How do you freeze a quarter while appeals for it can still arrive for {{appeal_days}} days?
A policy area is split in two from next quarter. How do you present a year of trend for each half?
With {{regions}} regions and {{policy_areas}} policy areas, many cells fall below {{min_cell}}. How do you choose which extra cells to suppress so totals stay published and nothing can be recovered?
A regulator asks you to prove that a published number matches your decisions. What do you show them, and what do you not need to show?

rules.ask: The quarter's published number and the dashboard differ by 0.3%. Which one is right, and how do you show it?
You suppress one region's cell for a policy area but publish the row total. How would a reader recover the suppressed value?
The report must also agree exactly with its own totals. Which numbers get noise, and how do you keep totals consistent?
Last quarter's file was downloaded thousands of times before you changed it. How does a reader learn what changed?
One old policy area became two new ones. How do you assign last year's decisions without guessing?

incidents: After publication, an audit finds that a pipeline change counted appeals restored by a later review twice for one quarter; the published restoration count for one region is 18% too high.

A policy area is split in two mid-quarter. Decisions before the split are counted under the old area and later ones under the new areas, so the quarter's file shows all three side by side, and readers comparing with last quarter conclude that actions in the old area fell by half.

A researcher shows that three suppressed cells for one region can be recovered from the published row and column totals, because suppression was applied per cell below {{min_cell}} without complementary cells.
The decision ledger's region field was backfilled from current account regions instead of the region at decision time; about 2% of last year's actions move between regions when the report is rerun.

templates.title: Protecting the well-being of a team whose work exposes them to distressing reports
templates.subtopic: exposure to distressing material, workload, support, delivery under pressure

trigger: two engineers spent three days opening reported items one by one to find the cause of a queue incident
an engineer quietly asked to stop working on the moderation tooling, and said others feel the same
the moderation programme announced a launch that will double, within a quarter, the number of reported items your pipelines and tools handle

sections.scenario: You lead a team of {{team_size}} engineers who build the data pipelines and tools behind moderation: report intake, queues, the reviewers' tooling and the metrics on decisions. The team is not a reviewing team, but debugging, testing and labelling problems sometimes mean opening reported items, and nothing limits how often. Recently, {{trigger}}. A major delivery for the moderation programme is due in {{weeks}} weeks.
sections.problem: What do you do? Cover the first conversations you have, how you reduce how much distressing material your team sees without stopping the work, what support you put in place and how people can use it without it counting against them, how you change the team's tools and practices (for example, what engineers can do without opening items at all), how you handle the delivery date, and how you will know whether things are better. Then tell me about a real time you looked after a team's well-being under pressure, with what happened, or say that you have not and reason it through. Describe processes and practices only; no example of content is needed or wanted.
sections.constraints: The delivery date matters to the moderation programme, and moving it has a cost to other teams. You are not a clinician. Support must be available to people who do not want their manager to know they are using it.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Listens first and privately, without probing for detail or diagnosing; treats exposure as a measurable risk and designs it down (access only when needed and logged, masked or synthetic data for debugging and tests, tools that show metadata instead of items, limits and rotation that apply to everyone); puts in place support people can use privately and normalises it; brings the delivery trade-off to the programme's leads with evidence and a scope proposal; measures outcomes in aggregate without forcing disclosure; describes processes only; real example with what changed and personal contribution, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Does the company offer support services for this kind of work?
clarifications.a: Assume a general employee support service exists; specialised support for this work is something you could ask for.

clarifications.q: Can engineers work on synthetic or masked data instead?
clarifications.a: For most debugging, in principle yes; nobody has built it.

clarifications.q: Has anyone said they are struggling?
clarifications.a: One person has said they are tired; nobody has said more, and you do not know how others feel.

clarifications.q: Who else needs to agree to changes?
clarifications.a: The moderation programme's leads for anything that changes the delivery, and the security and privacy teams for changes to who can open items.

hints: Treat exposure as something you can measure and design down, like any other risk: who opens items, how often, and why.
Separate what needs a decision from you this week from what needs tooling over months.
Support works when using it is normal and private; make the team's practices model that, starting with you.
followups: What do you say in the first one-to-one conversations, and what do you avoid saying?
Which work can be done without opening a reported item, and what would you build to make that possible?
The delivery is at risk because you have reduced exposure. How do you make the case to the programme's leads?
How would you measure whether the changes helped, without asking people to disclose more than they want?
In your real example, what did you get wrong at first, and what changed afterwards?

rules.ask: Your two most experienced engineers are the ones who can debug the queue fastest. Does rotation apply to them too, and what does it cost the delivery?
Someone answers that they are fine but you see signs they are not. What do you do, and what do you not do?
A bug only reproduces on a real reported item. Who may open it, under what rules, and who knows it happened?
The programme's leads say the date cannot move. What scope do you cut, and who decides?
Which decision did you personally make, and how did you tell the team?

templates.title: A launch that must work in dozens of languages on day one
templates.subtopic: localisation, per-language quality bars, go/no-go, cross-team coordination

feature: auto-generated captions that creators can edit
comment filters creators set by keyword
a new in-app editor with text effects
gap: right-to-left scripts have never been tested in the pipeline
quality has been measured for only five languages
half the languages have so little test data that no metric is stable

sections.scenario: The launch of {{feature}} is planned for {{languages}} languages on the same day, {{weeks}} weeks from now, and the date has been announced to creators. You lead the data and engineering work behind it: the pipelines, the quality measurement and the launch metrics. Today, {{gap}}. Localisation, product, and regional teams in several time zones each own part of the launch.
sections.problem: How would you lead it? Cover how you find out what "works" means for each language, how you measure quality where data is thin, what you build or test first, how you coordinate teams across time zones, what decides whether each language launches on the day, and what you monitor after launch. Then tell me about a real launch you led or worked on that had to work across many languages, markets or locales, with what happened, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: The date is public. Launching a language that works badly harms creators who rely on it. You cannot hire speakers of every language in {{weeks}} weeks, but regional teams can help.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Defines a per-language quality bar of the same shape before measuring; finds the classes of language that break pipelines (script direction, segmentation, character sets, formats) and tests one of each early; measures quality with stated confidence where data is thin, using regional teams with a clear method; coordinates across time zones with owners and handoffs; decides per language with criteria set in advance, recommends a phased launch honestly where needed and explains it to creators; monitors per-language signals after launch with a switch per language; real example with what changed and personal contribution, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Can some languages launch later?
clarifications.a: Yes, if you make the case. Product prefers all on the day.

clarifications.q: Who judges quality in a language nobody on the team speaks?
clarifications.a: Regional teams and contracted reviewers can, if you give them a clear method and enough of their time.

clarifications.q: Are there language-specific rules?
clarifications.a: Some: scripts written right to left, languages without spaces between words, and different number and date formats.

clarifications.q: Is there a fallback when a language is not ready?
clarifications.a: The feature can be hidden per language with a switch.

hints: Write the quality bar per language before measuring anything, and make it the same shape for every language even if the numbers differ.
Find the classes of language that break things (script direction, word segmentation, character sets) and test one of each first.
Decide in advance, per language, what launches, what waits, and who signs off.
followups: How do you measure quality for a language with very little test data, and how confident can you be?
Two weeks before launch, eight languages are below the bar. What do you recommend, and how do you present it?
How do you run a launch day across teams in many time zones without one person awake for 24 hours?
After launch, one language's creators turn the feature off at three times the rate of others. What do you do?
In your real example, which language or market surprised you, and what did you change afterwards?

rules.ask: Who checks that a translated test set measures the same thing as the original, and how?
The metric is fine for one language but creators there complain. What is your metric missing?
The date was announced for all {{languages}} languages. How do you explain a phased launch to the creators who wait?
Who can turn off one language at 3 a.m. their time, and what tells them to?
Which call did you personally make, and what did it cost?

templates.title: Keeping data quality when the product changes every week
templates.subtopic: event contracts, release cadence, ownership, prevention over detection

symptom: a creator-facing metric dipped for two days after an app release renamed an event field
a LIVE metric doubled after a client started sending an event twice on reconnect
upload success rates were wrong for a week because a new app version added a step that nobody mapped
authority: you lead the data platform team
you are a senior engineer on the analytics team with no authority over the app teams
a director has given you a quarter to fix this

sections.scenario: The app ships a new version every week. {{teams}} product teams add and change the events their features send. Last month, {{breakages}} metrics were wrong for at least a day after releases; the latest: {{symptom}}. Each time, the data team found out from someone downstream, and fixed it by hand. In this situation, {{authority}}. The product teams' priority is shipping, and they see data checks as something that slows them down.
sections.problem: How would you change this? Cover how you find where breakages come from, what you change so they are caught before release rather than after, who owns an event and its definition, how you make the change cheap for product teams, what you measure to know it is working, and how you get teams to adopt it. Then tell me about a real time you improved data quality in a fast-changing product, with what happened, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: The weekly release cadence does not change. You cannot block releases on your own authority. The fixes must not need a data engineer in every product team.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Diagnoses breakages by cause before prescribing; moves checks to where changes are made (event definitions in code, schema validation and count checks in app tests and pre-release builds) rather than only downstream monitoring; defines ownership with a lineage of who depends on each event and a compatible-change policy (add, deprecate, then remove); makes the safe path easy for product teams and earns adoption without blocking authority; measures quality (breakages per release, time to detect, metrics wrong per month) and shows the trend; real example with what changed and personal contribution, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Is there a schema for events today?
clarifications.a: Loosely: a shared document that is out of date.

clarifications.q: Do product teams test their events?
clarifications.a: Some check that an event fires; none check its fields or its counts.

clarifications.q: Who notices broken metrics now?
clarifications.a: Usually an analyst or a creator support team, days later.

clarifications.q: Is there budget for tooling?
clarifications.a: Some, if you can show what it saves.

hints: Classify the last few breakages by cause. The fix for a renamed field is different from the fix for a duplicated event.
Move checks to where the change is made: the event definition and the app's tests, not the warehouse.
Make the safe path the easy one for product teams; adoption follows convenience more than mandates.
followups: What did your classification of the breakages show, and which fix comes first?
How do you define ownership of an event so that a change cannot ship without its owner knowing what depends on it?
A product team says your new check delayed their release by a day. What do you do?
What would you measure to show leadership that quality improved, and how long before you could tell?
In your real example, what did teams resist, and how did you change your approach?

rules.ask: A team needs to rename a field this week for a launch. What does your contract let them do, and what happens to the dashboards that read the old name?
Your alert fires two days after release, like the analysts did. What would catch it before release?
You cannot block releases. How does your check stop a breaking change without that authority?
Deduplication downstream hides the client bug. Who finds out the client sends events twice, and how?
What did you personally build or change, and what did others do?

templates.title: Another team presents your team's work as its own
templates.subtopic: credit, recognition for the team, direct conversation, escalation judgement

work: the pipeline that made upload success visible per app version for the first time
the sound-licence checks that stopped videos playing sounds after their licence ended
the creator rewards restatement process that fixed months of support tickets
venue: a quarterly review with senior leadership
a written launch announcement sent to the whole organisation
who: a partner team you depend on for the next quarter
a team whose lead is your manager's peer
a team that contributed a small part of the work

sections.scenario: Your team spent a quarter building {{work}}. In {{venue}}, {{who}} presented the result as their own work, without mentioning your team. Two of your engineers saw it and are upset; one of them wrote most of the code and is hoping for a promotion this cycle. You need that other team's cooperation for next quarter's plan.
sections.problem: What do you do? Cover what you do first, how you find out whether it was deliberate or an oversight, how you raise it with the other team, what you do for your own engineers, whether and how you involve your manager, and how you make sure your team's work is visible in future. Then tell me about a real time credit for your or your team's work went elsewhere, or you saw it happen to someone else, with what happened, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: You need the other team next quarter. The promotion decision is not yours alone. The presentation cannot be undone.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Assumes good faith first and checks the facts; talks to the other team's lead privately and directly, asking for a specific, proportionate fix (credit in the next update, a correction in the written record) that keeps the relationship; puts the engineers first: tells them what will be done, and makes sure the promotion evidence reflects their work through the right channel; involves the manager in proportion, as information or for help, not as a complaint; builds visibility into future work (written design docs and launch notes with authors, shared presentations); real example with what happened and personal contribution, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Did the other team contribute anything?
clarifications.a: Some integration work and the launch communication.

clarifications.q: Has this happened before with this team?
clarifications.a: Not that you know of.

clarifications.q: Do your engineers want you to do something?
clarifications.a: One wants a correction announced; the other wants it dropped.

clarifications.q: Does your manager know?
clarifications.a: Not yet.

hints: Assume an oversight until you know otherwise, and ask before you conclude.
Separate two goals: your engineers' work being recognised where it matters, and a good working relationship with the other team.
Visibility is easier to build in than to repair: think about how work gets written up and presented in future.
followups: What exactly do you say to the other team's lead, and what outcome do you ask for?
The other team's lead says the presentation simplified things and no harm was done. What now?
How do you make sure the engineer who wrote most of the code gets recognised for the promotion decision?
The same thing happens again a quarter later. What changes in your approach?
In your real example, what did you do, and what would you do differently now?

rules.ask: What do you ask your manager to do, and what would you consider a good outcome?
A public correction embarrasses a team you need next quarter. Is there another way to get the same result?
Your engineer who wrote most of the code asks you why you did nothing. What do you say?
Who reads that write-up, and will it reach the people deciding the promotion?
What did you personally do or say, and when?

templates.title: Project deep dive, re-examined for short-video creation, LIVE and community at global scale
templates.subtopic: design decisions, failures, late mobile data, regional rules and creator-visible numbers

angle: the data model and the keys
the hardest failure you diagnosed in it
the decision you would most like to undo
requirement: uploads retried and resumed over unreliable mobile networks counted once
LIVE gift totals on screen that match creators' statements exactly
rules that differ by region, such as sound licences, applied per country and as of a date
viewers appearing only in aggregates, with a creator seeing only their own numbers
scale: hundreds of millions of uploads a month

sections.scenario: In this part of the loop you describe a data system you designed or substantially changed, one that other teams or customers depended on. The interviewer will go deep on {{angle}}, then ask how the system would have to change for short-video creation, LIVE and community, at a scale of {{scale}}, with {{requirement}}.
sections.problem: Give a five-minute overview: the problem, the users, the scale in numbers, the architecture and your role. Then go deep on {{angle}}. Then reason through what changes at a scale of {{scale}}, with {{requirement}}. If you have never owned such a system, say so, pick the closest thing you have worked on, and be clear about which parts you are reasoning through rather than recalling.
sections.constraints: Your own project only. Describe it without revealing anything a previous employer would not want shared; round numbers are fine if you say so.
sections.assumptions: The short-video setting is hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Clear problem framing with real numbers; depth on the chosen angle down to keys, schemas and failure modes; decisions explained with alternatives and evidence; honest account of what broke and what changed; a credible re-examination that names the assumptions that would not survive the scale and addresses {{requirement}} incrementally (for example client-generated upload ids with idempotent processing and late mobile events counted on their event date; an append-only gift ledger with the on-screen total as a projection reconciled after the session; versioned regional rules joined as of the event date; aggregates with minimum group sizes and creator views scoped to the creator); own contribution clearly separated from the team's, or an honest statement of reasoning rather than recall.

clarifications.q: Does it have to be a video or social system?
clarifications.a: No. Any system that moved, stored or computed data others depended on; the re-examination is where we bring it into this domain.

clarifications.q: Can it be a team project?
clarifications.a: Yes, but separate what you did from what the team did.

clarifications.q: How deep should I go?
clarifications.a: Down to keys, schemas, failure modes and numbers.

hints: Lead with the problem and the numbers before the architecture.
Have one decision you would defend again and one you would change.
For the re-examination, start from one event (an upload, a gift, a comment): where it is created, which ids it carries, and which of them the new requirement constrains.
followups: What was the main alternative to your key design decision, and what evidence chose between them?
What broke in production, how did you find out, and what did you change?
Which parts of your design would not survive a scale of {{scale}}? What breaks first?
How would you provide {{requirement}} without a rewrite?
What would you build differently today, and why?

rules.ask: Which parts did you personally design or write?
Is that per day or in total, and what was the peak relative to the average?
A phone retries an upload five times over a day on a bad connection. Where in your design is it counted, and how many times?
A rule changes in one country on a date. Which of your tables know which rule applied to an event a month ago?
Who can see a single viewer's activity in your design, and why?
